item.title: He Was China’s Man in Panama. Then He Became a Wanted Man.
item.description:
For years, Zhang Liang warned that powerful people in his former homeland, China, would try to drag him back. Then one Saturday morning in July, it happened.

In Panama City, two police officers on motorbikes pulled alongside his black Mercedes-Benz and motioned him to stop. A check of his identification turned up an Interpol red notice from the Chinese authorities, who wanted him extradited on charges of embezzling around $300 million.

Mr. Zhang, a 44-year-old dealmaker, barely had time to remove his gray suit jacket and wrap it around his head before officers handcuffed him and paraded him before cameras at Interpol’s National Central Bureau in Panama.

He has been behind bars ever since.

It was a remarkable fall for Mr. Zhang, one that traces the arc of China’s dealings with the West. He went to Panama ready to make deals and help China extend its influence. He oversaw a port project that promised to turn a former U.S. military base near the Panama Canal’s Atlantic entrance into Latin America’s largest container terminal, establishing a base for Chinese interests near one of the world’s busiest trade routes.

Today, China’s ruling Communist Party holds much tighter reins on entrepreneurs like Mr. Zhang. At the same time, Panama has been caught in a showdown between the United States and China: President Trump claims that China exercises too much control over the Panama Canal.

Mr. Zhang believes he is a pawn in a larger political game — a way for Beijing to regain direct control over key infrastructure he helped build in Panama.

“China is seeing its influence in the Panama Canal slipping away and is now putting pressure on Panama,” Mr. Zhang said from prison in a letter responding to written questions from The New York Times.

To his aggrieved former business partners, though, Mr. Zhang is a corporate fugitive who used offshore jurisdictions and other people’s money to enrich himself. He wooed Panama’s elite with promises of deals and funding that never materialized. He continued to earn a salary of $6,300 a month, his lawyers said at a bail hearing, a substantial sum in Panama.

His tailored suits, A. Lange & Söhne wristwatch and black Mercedes all pointed to a lavish lifestyle. Mr. Zhang has faced lawsuits, criminal complaints and judicial proceedings in multiple jurisdictions. He is also pursuing an international arbitration claim against Panama.

The competing accounts of victim and culprit are difficult to reconcile. The ownership of the port is disputed, and the financial dealings behind it are opaque. After reviewing the case, Panama’s Foreign Affairs Ministry agreed last month to proceed with Mr. Zhang’s extradition to China, according to a document seen by The Times.

The Foreign Affairs Ministries of China and Panama did not respond to emailed questions.

For a decade, Mr. Zhang had used China’s growing interest in Panama to expand his influence. Now, as Beijing and Washington battle over the canal, his business empire has unraveled, and the political connections that once helped him prosper offer little protection.

This account, with previously unreported details, is based on official documents, legal filings and interviews with lawyers and associates, including a former colleague who has accused local authorities in China of harassment, coercion and the falsifying of records in Mr. Zhang’s case.

Mr. Zhang arrived in Panama in 2016 to oversee investments for a wealthy Chinese financier. A lawyer licensed in New York and China, he had been named a “leading talent” by China’s Justice Ministry.

From an 18th-floor office overlooking Panama Bay, Mr. Zhang secured Panama’s approval to build, own and operate a major container terminal in a free-trade zone on Margarita Island.

Chinese state-controlled media celebrated the deal as a diplomatic coup, advancing investment interests in Panama. Mr. Zhang also secured a deal to build a gas-fired power plant. He promised officials that the project would create 1,000 jobs and lower energy costs.

As deals were made, Mr. Zhang became a go-between for officials in Beijing and Panama City.

His success coincided with Beijing’s courtship of Juan Carlos Varela, who was Panama’s president. In 2017, Panama severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan and aligned with China. It also became the first Latin American country to join the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s signature global infrastructure program.

Washington watched the growing relationship with alarm. Mr. Zhang’s proposed terminal would sit beside the Panama Canal, a strategic artery for the United States.

“Margarita Island gave them a lot of access and intelligence value,” said Isaac B. Kardon, an adjunct professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who specializes in Chinese maritime strategy.

But the political opening started to close.

Mr. Varela left office in 2019, and his successor was far less receptive to Chinese investment. The Panamanian government began moving against the Margarita Island project.

Mr. Zhang sought Beijing’s help. Tingyun Han, his former assistant and translator, said she had gone to the Chinese Embassy in Panama City, hoping officials could persuade the Panamanian government to reconsider. The plea went nowhere.

The new Panamanian government “no longer wanted any Asian faces or Chinese enterprises involved,” Ms. Han told The Times from China.

Mr. Zhang’s problems deepened when his backer, a wealthy property financier named Gao Tianguo, lost his fortune. Mr. Gao’s lending businesses in China collapsed under billions of dollars of debt. He was arrested in 2020 and died two years later.

In 2022, Mr. Zhang agreed to transfer the port assets to Notarc Management Group, a Bahamas and Florida-based private equity firm. Within months, the deal incited an ownership dispute. Ye Cheng, a politically connected Chinese businessman who claimed a controlling stake in the project, accused Mr. Zhang of illegally seizing the company.

But Panamanian authorities declined to bring charges, concluding that Mr. Ye’s allegations amounted to a commercial dispute. Mr. Ye’s company, the Landbridge Group, did not reply to requests for comment.

China took a different view.

In 2023, police officers pulled Ms. Han, Mr. Zhang’s former assistant, off a plane in her home city of Xian and drove her 12 hours to Rizhao, where Mr. Ye’s company has its headquarters, she said. Officers interrogated her so intensely about Mr. Zhang and the port deal, she said, that she vomited and was taken to a hospital. She later accused the local police of torture.

Mr. Zhang became convinced that his adversaries in China were coming after him. In court filings in 2024, he described being followed to work by a white Nissan and chased through Panama City. He requested and received police protection.

By the time the police stopped Mr. Zhang’s Mercedes in July, Panama had become the focus of tensions between Washington and Beijing.

Shortly after starting his second term, President Trump demanded that Panama loosen China’s grip on the Panama Canal. He accused a Hong Kong conglomerate that operated two major ports at the canal, one at either end, of being controlled by Beijing. In January, Panama’s Supreme Court declared the company’s port contract unconstitutional.

China vowed to “take all necessary measures” to defend its interests in Panama. Chinese authorities started detaining hundreds of Panamanian-flagged vessels in China for inspection, disrupting trade.

Mr. Zhang was arrested the same week that China’s new ambassador arrived in Panama — and just five days before Panamanian officials were due in Beijing for talks to defuse the diplomatic standoff.

Panama’s foreign minister later said China had renewed a key maritime agreement that grants Panamanian-flagged ships preferential access to its ports.

“From the moment they arrested him — and that is no coincidence — the disputes between China and Panama disappeared,” said Guillermo Cochez, a Panamanian diplomat and one of Mr. Zhang’s lawyers.

No evidence links his arrest to the diplomatic negotiations. But relations between China and Panama improved afterward. Extradition documents revealed that Beijing wanted control of Mr. Zhang’s assets in Panama without explicitly asking for the port project.

On Aug. 21, a Panamanian court denied Mr. Zhang bail and ruled that the seriousness of the charges outweighed his claims of personal roots in Panama. In September, Panama’s Foreign Ministry said China’s extradition request was “appropriate.”

Mr. Zhang was moved from La Gran Joya, a high-security prison outside Panama City, to another detention center nearby, while his lawyers pursue a final appeal.

China has said Mr. Zhang is a Chinese national, although he said he had renounced his Chinese citizenship and obtained citizenship from Saint Lucia in 2020. The Times reviewed copies of his permanent residency card, his Saint Lucia passport and his Chinese passport.

Chinese authorities said Mr. Zhang’s transfer of the port terminal to Notarc had constituted embezzlement. He dismissed the allegations as a “sham.” (Notarc also sued him, seeking compensation for losses it says it incurred in the dispute.) Notarc did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Zhang said the criminal case was a pretext for Beijing to seize the Margarita Island project and “get back into the canal.”

But, he warned, “what Panama doesn’t realize is the pressure won’t stop with extraditing me.”

item.title: Behind the All-American Ralph Lauren Brand Is a French C.E.O.
item.description:
Ralph Lauren is going through a renaissance.

But when Patrice Louvet took over as chief executive in 2017, the company was at a low point. His predecessor, the first chief of the firm not named Ralph Lauren, stepped down after a little more than a year amid creative clashes with the eponymous founder.

Mr. Louvet, 62, was an unexpected choice. Born in France, he served in the French Navy and spent nearly 30 years at Procter & Gamble, known for selling razors and shampoo, not polo shirts and knit sweaters.

Under his leadership, the brand started relying less on heavy discounting and pulled out of lower-tier stores. Its preppy look is once again popular with young people. Reservations are essential at its packed restaurants, and at the coffee shops, the lines are long. The company’s share price has risen more than 400 percent since Mr. Louvet took the top job.

Last fiscal year, Ralph Lauren brought in $8.1 billion in revenue, a 14 percent increase. It recently raised its forecast for sales and profit margins for the current year, ahead of the holiday shopping season.

Like other retailers, Ralph Lauren must try to remain relevant as trends shift rapidly and politics increasingly intrudes on culture. The company has many stakeholders, but the Lauren family controls more than 80 percent of the vote among shareholders.

Mr. Louvet has picked up many lessons from Mr. Lauren, 87, who is chief creative officer and executive chairman, that have helped guide him on where to take the brand next.

“In this industry, if all you do is magic, then you can build a nice little business, but it’s not going to go very far,” Mr. Louvet said. “If all you do is logic, you can’t be successful in this industry.” Success, he says, is striking a balance between the two.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

People want to know the relationship that you have with Ralph Lauren, the man. How do you work together?

One of the key reasons I left Procter & Gamble is the opportunity to work with Ralph. There are very few visionary philanthropists, entrepreneurs, innovators like him.

We took a lot of time to understand each other as humans, not as businesspeople, before we both signed in May 2017.

We never documented what our respective roles were.

All the McKinsey people right now are lifting their heads and saying, “What?”

Yeah, exactly. No job description. Instinctively, intuitively, we got clear on our respective lanes.

Ralph is very focused on the creative vision of the company. I focus on just running the company and delivering for the near term and the long term.

How has the relationship changed?

The nature of the relationship with Ralph hasn’t changed dramatically. If anything, we’ve become really close friends. We have lunch together every week when we’re not traveling. We might spend two, three hours together and not a minute on business.

The trust has been built over time. There’s been very few situations where we weren’t aligned from the get-go on specific decisions, which is pretty unique 10 years in.

Ralph talks about magic and gut instinct, and you come from an operational background focused on logic and spreadsheets. What’s an example of when you two differed on a business decision?

We did a beautiful fashion show and the theme was “Ralph’s Club.” Janelle Monáe was there, she sang and she got on the tables. It was spectacular. Black tie. After that, Ralph said: “Let’s open a club. I love that spirit, that atmosphere. Magic.”

But the financials made no sense. Ralph, as he often is, was very passionate about it. We ultimately decided this is when the logic needs to override the magic.

The American flag has always played a role in the Ralph Lauren brand. How do you protect what feels essential about the brand while also not having it be politicized?

This company has been around for 60 years. We focus on values that ultimately are universal values, not political values: optimism, authenticity, quality, entrepreneurship, family. The brand is resonating so well in Sydney, in Shanghai, in Chicago, because these values resonate with everyone around the world.

Our business internationally is actually even stronger than it is in the U.S. China is up 35 percent. We’ve been growing north of 20 percent for several years, at a time where the geopolitical situation is tense between those two markets. This is true across every market.

Is it possible to bring clothing production to the United States?

We are keen to bring production to the U.S. We manufacture all our Olympic gear here, as we get ready for the L.A. 2028 Olympics, which will be a big moment for our company. We manufacture a number of our luxury products here. There’s a manufacturing site in Queens.

Our products are pretty sophisticated. I don’t think we want to necessarily drive massive T-shirt manufacturing in the U.S. But certainly the intent is there, the interest is there.

Trend-wise, Ralph is back. But what happens if the fashion cycle changes?

Ralph has many wonderful quotes, including this one: “I don’t want to be too hot and I don’t want to be too cold.” We’re not looking to chase trends.

The majority of our business — more than 70 percent — is our core products that are available year in, year out. We might evolve the color, we might evolve the sizing. It might be a bit oversized or it might be slim fit. But that tweed jacket, that white polo shirt, that rugby shirt, that cable knit sweater, those are staples that stay all year and across time.

One of the pivots we made when we started this journey 10 years ago is to be much more consumer centric. The younger generation was on TikTok. We couldn’t spell TikTok. They were shopping on e-commerce platforms. We weren’t there. They were gaming. We weren’t there.

And we said, “If we want to talk to that young generation and bring them in, let’s understand where they want to engage with brands, where they want to shop, and let’s make sure we’re there in a way that’s consistent with our brand image.”

Many young people are finding the brand through the secondary market. Some brands see the secondhand clothing market as diluting a brand. But your company recently hosted PoloFest, an event selling vintage Ralph clothes, in Tokyo.

Ralph has always been about timelessness. The vision is for products to be handed down, for the father to hand it to his son, for grandmother to hand to the granddaughter.

A lot of people discover our brand, particularly the younger generation now, through secondary markets, which is pretty neat. They become part of that ecosystem, and then ultimately come to our store at full price. You will see a lot of vintage in our stores.

Tell me about your upbringing. You were born in France.

I was born in a little town called Saint-Cloud, just outside Paris. My father was an engineer and worked for a French chemical company. My mother was a homemaker and she did philanthropic activities. I’m the eldest of four.

What was a formative time in your childhood?

When I was 9, my father was sent to New Jersey. I was not particularly excited to leave my friends, my school, my activities, my environment. I was thrown into American public school, not speaking any English. The first few months were rough.

My father had studied at M.I.T., so he knew a little bit of the U.S., but my three siblings, my mom and I were all discovering the U.S. at the same time. I think there’s strength in everyone going through the same experience.

You spent nearly 30 years at P&G. I read that an employee once told you that you were not the right leader. How did that affect you?

It was a massive gut punch. I was in charge of hair care and health care in Japan and Korea, my first general manager role. I am sent there with a very clear mission: to turn the business around. I came in all guns blazing with a sense of urgency.

I learned you must clarify the direction and the vision. It was clear in my head, but I had not really democratized it. Define it overtly and then make sure you’re engaging everyone around it. Don’t move before you’ve done that.

It’s time for the lightning round. What do you wear to feel most confident?

What you’re seeing today. A blue pinstriped suit. Ralph Lauren watch — also available in women’s.

What’s one fashion trend you cannot stand?

White socks and slides.

What are you personally trying to learn right now?

Artificial intelligence, particularly agents.

What’s the last question you asked A.I.?

I asked it last night, what were the drivers to the stock price decline after earnings.

How do you sign off to your emails?

Onwards and upwards, together.

What’s one place that you think people should still be wearing ties but aren’t?

We should be wearing ties everywhere.

Tell me about an object in your office and the significance of it.

Someone from my team gave me a little Yoda. This is an industry where there’s a lot of emotion. There’s a good amount of intensity. Yoda is a good reminder to just breathe and don’t overreact.

item.title: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left the Company in August 2025
item.description:
Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center company, said on Sunday that Alice Huang, a former executive at the center of what U.S. officials call a Chinese spy plot targeting the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, had left the company in August 2025, according to a company statement.

The statement, which was reported by The Associated Press, was Megaspeed’s first to directly address the status of Ms. Huang since she became the focus of international scrutiny over her ties to Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday.

News of their relationship rocked Nvidia, the dominant maker of artificial intelligence chips, as well as the global technology sector and the U.S. government.

Last month, The New York Times reported that American officials had concluded Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and had a close relationship with Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom and an adviser to President Trump.

Mr. Huang acknowledged last Sunday that he had had an affair with Ms. Huang, and Nvidia’s board of directors said they had begun an investigation into his conduct. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that he also had an extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. He abruptly stepped down as chief executive the next day from the company he had led for more than 30 years.

The chip maker’s stock has fallen about 30 percent below its all-time high, which was set just over a month ago, erasing more than $1 trillion in market value.

The scandal has trained attention on Megaspeed, a small company that purchased billions of dollars of Nvidia’s coveted chips from 2024 to 2026.

That set off an investigation by the U.S. Department of Commerce as to whether some of the chips were funneled to China, in possible violation of American export restrictions. The United States has not lodged any formal charges against the company.

On Thursday, Megaspeed’s chief executive, James Tan, said in a statement that the company had not broken U.S. laws, had cooperated with Commerce Department investigators and was “ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”

Megaspeed’s statement on Sunday reiterated that its business was “legitimate and lawful” and for the first time mentioned Ms. Huang, who helped set up the company starting in 2023, saying she had no current role there.

“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters,” it told The A.P. in an emailed statement.

“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” the company added.

Still, the statement added to the emerging timeline involving Ms. Huang, who has not responded to requests for comment. China has denied the espionage claims.

The Times reported in October 2025 that Ms. Huang had stepped down from the company months earlier, citing a human resources manager, though it was unclear where she went.

Last week, the government of Singapore said it had confiscated Ms. Huang’s passport from June 2025 to February 2026 over “potential false declarations” about Megaspeed. She was ultimately released and barred from re-entering Singapore.

U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, had informed Mr. Trump of concerns about Ms. Huang and her relationship with Mr. Huang as early as October 2025.

Mr. Trump declined to take action. This May, Mr. Trump brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China, another sign of Mr. Huang’s importance to the A.I. data center boom that is a key driver of the American economy.

The scandal has touched off a new round infighting in the Trump administration over its approach to A.I. and China.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a prominent voice in favor of allowing U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell products in Asia, has faced accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that his department has been too cozy with Nvidia and Mr. Huang.

Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, said on Friday that his department and others had supported putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but that only the Commerce Department could take that step. The Commerce Department said that such a move would be an administration-wide decision.

Mr. Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside itself for a new chief executive. On “Sunday Morning Futures” on Fox News, he said that the company needs “a dramatic shake-up.”

He added that the company’s board and outside counsel within the next 10 days needed to answer questions ​about the company’s culture of compliance with export ⁠restrictions.

Adeel Hassan contributed reporting.

item.title: F.D.A. Rejects Closely Watched Lung Cancer Drug From China
item.description:
The Food and Drug Administration rejected a first-of-its-kind cancer drug that was invented in China, a setback for a medicine that had become a symbol of China’s ascendance as a powerhouse in drug development.

Summit Therapeutics, the Florida company that has been seeking to bring the drug to the American market, disclosed the agency’s decision in a news release on Sunday. Summit bought the U.S. rights to the drug from Akeso Biopharma, a Chinese drugmaker that invented the drug in its laboratories and sells it in China.

Summit had been seeking approval only for certain patients with advanced lung cancer. But the drug had raised high hopes because it is being tested in many more cancers, including tumors of the colon, bladder and breast.

Summit said on Sunday that the F.D.A. told the company it had rejected the drug because it had not shown a statistically significant benefit in prolonging patients’ lives in the global clinical trial that was the basis of Summit’s application.

Summit had been seeking F.D.A. approval based on the results of a study the company conducted in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia that enrolled patients who had already tried a targeted treatment. The trial compared patients who received ivonescimab and chemotherapy with those whose only treatment was chemotherapy. In that study, the drug was successful in delaying the cancer’s progression.

Summit has argued that the failure to extend patients’ lives simply reflected slow enrollment in the study. Hoping to bolster its case, the company had sent the F.D.A. analyses that were not specified in the original research plan of patients’ longer-time outcomes, but those were not enough to persuade regulators.

The F.D.A. did not return a request for comment on its decision, as is typical with rejections.

The drug, given as an intravenous infusion, is novel because it combines two attacks on a tumor. It unleashes the immune system with one strategy and deprives the tumor of a blood supply with another. Large drugmakers like Merck and Pfizer are developing medicines that take the same approach.

Ivonescimab’s boosters had hoped that the drug would eventually displace Keytruda, the world’s best-selling cancer medicine that is used to treat a broad range of cancer types. But cancer researchers around the world have said that the clinical trial results so far have not justified such widespread use.

The rejection comes as a flurry of promising experimental drugs are emerging from Chinese laboratories and fueling fierce debate about whether the United States is ceding its longstanding dominance in biotechnology to China.

People who support the activity point out that American patients can benefit from Chinese innovation. But Chinese drugmakers face fewer regulatory hurdles and can move more quickly than their American counterparts, a dynamic that some American lawmakers, investors and executives say puts U.S. companies at a deep disadvantage.

And as more medicines show promise in clinical trials in China, researchers around the world have voiced concern that drugs may not work as well in American patients as they do in Chinese patients, for reasons that are not fully understood. American regulators have insisted on seeing data in Western populations before approving cancer drugs from China.

For decades, the world’s top-selling drugs were generally invented in laboratories in the United States or Europe. China was seen as a sleepy manufacturer of generic medicines and drug ingredients. But that has been changing as China’s biotechnology industry has surged in recent years, churning out patents, papers and cutting-edge experimental drugs.

The blood cancer medications Brukinsa and Carvykti were invented in China and now generate over $1 billion in annual revenue in the United States.

To bring drugs invented in China to American patients, Chinese companies sometimes sell the U.S. rights to American drugmakers, as Akeso and Summit did with ivonescimab. These types of deals would continue to be permitted under new proposed regulations from the Trump administration prohibiting U.S. companies and investors from taking investment stakes in Chinese biotechnology.

Around the globe, ivonescimab is being tested in 17 continuing, completed or planned late-stage studies, according to Summit.

Most of interest to cancer researchers is a clinical trial of ivonescimab that is expected to report results before the end of this year. That study enrolled patients in the United States, China and other countries who have not yet tried a treatment for their advanced lung cancer. It will assess whether ivonescimab is better than Keytruda at prolonging lives and extending the time until cancer progresses.

If that study succeeds, Summit is expected to seek F.D.A. approval for the drug to be used in that setting.

In the news release on Sunday, Bob Duggan, a co-chief executive officer of Summit, said that even with the F.D.A.’s decision, “nothing changes with respect to our ever-growing belief in the opportunity for ivonescimab and our determination to advance ivonescimab’s development.”

item.title: Black Friday is Coming. Bring on the Travel Deals!
item.description:
This year, the Black Friday sales season — from early November through Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Travel Tuesday and sometimes beyond — promises big savings. Agencies like Expedia and brands like Hilton are offering extensive sales, as usual, but so are ski country lodges, wellness retreats and cruise lines with new ships.

That’s good news for travelers. In a fall survey by the research firm MMGY Travel Intelligence, more than half of the respondents said travel had become less affordable over the past year. More than four in five said they had taken or planned to adopt a money-saving strategy such as driving instead of flying.

To sort through the deals, make a shopping list. And scrutinize the fine print. Often, deals are prepaid, nonrefundable and fleeting. At hotels, minimum-stay requirements of two nights or more are on the rise.

Offered in the coming weeks, the following deals are poised to appeal to a broad spectrum of shoppers.

Black Friday is a good time to look for a good deal on a new hotel.

Outbound Hotels, in mountain and desert destinations across the country, will include its two newest properties, Outbound Yosemite in Northern California and Outbound Park City in Park City, Utah, both opening next spring. The sale, from Nov. 17 to Dec. 3, will take up to 40 percent off rooms for travel throughout 2027. Rates across the portfolio will run from about $150 to $550 a night after the discount.

In Healdsburg, Calif., the Cottages at Little Saint, affiliated with the popular vegan restaurant Little Saint, will offer 15 percent off stays of three nights or more at its four cottages, which feature ebullient décor by the celebrated designer Ken Fulk. The sale runs Nov. 27 to Dec. 1 for travel from Dec. 1 to March 31. Rooms normally start at $400 a night.

The boutique hotel collection Lark, which this year opened the Cambridge Common House and the Drew Hotel in Massachusetts and the Penny Lane in the Hamptons, will hold a sale Nov. 25 to 28. It will take 30 percent off stays of two to four nights and up to 50 percent off bookings of five nights or more for travel through Nov. 18, 2027. Nightly rates normally start at $140 at the Drew in Plymouth.

Among a wave of wellness offers, the year-old Laugaras Lagoon in Iceland will hold its first Black Friday sale, offering 20 percent off gift cards Nov. 26 through 30. The cards can be redeemed for admission to the thermal lagoon, on the Golden Circle (entry starts around $59).

A new wellness resort in the Caribbean, TheLifeCo St. Lucia, will offer rooms at 30 percent off Nov. 20 to Dec. 2 for travel Dec. 1 to May 31. Before the discount, average nightly rates start at $600 and include meals, a medical consultation, yoga classes and treatments such as vibration therapy.

In Carefree, Ariz., Civana Wellness Resort & Spa is offering discounts of up to 50 percent on stays of two nights or more between Nov. 21 and the end of 2027 when booked Nov. 19 to Dec. 2. Nightly rates start at $349 before the sale and include meals, some hikes and many fitness classes.

Even high-end resorts can’t resist getting in on the buzz.

Cowboy up at the Meadows on Rock Creek, an all-inclusive, 2,000-acre guest ranch in western Montana, during its sale Nov. 27 to Dec. 15. Stays booked for three nights or longer during the 2027 season (May 25 to Oct. 31), will be discounted 20 percent (double occupancy cabins normally run $2,750 a night). Stays include meals and two activities — such as horseback riding and fly fishing — a day.

Stay Ombi operates three floating bungalows in Key Largo, Fla., that come with kayaks and paddleboards. Rates of roughly $1,000 a night will be discounted by 30 percent during its sale Nov. 23 to 30 for stays of two nights or more from Jan. 4 to Dec. 16, 2027 (use code BLACKFRIDAY30).

Safari-seekers can shop for rates 28 to 36 percent off at the new Kanana Nyana safari camp in the Okavango Delta in Botswana through March 31. Run by the travel company Ker & Downey, the boutique property offers four suites with private plunge pools overlooking the Xudum River and its floodplains. Rates, which normally start at $770 a person per night, include meals and game drives.

In the swanky Mayfair neighborhood of London, the Stafford hotel is running a sale that extends beyond rooms to its afternoon tea, priced at £61.60 (about $83), down 30 percent from £88. Book Nov. 23 to Dec. 3 for tea and scones Nov. 24 to May 9.

Black Friday and the ensuing few months known as “wave season” are a good time to look for discounted cruises.

Margaritaville at Sea is offering 60 percent off departures through 2028. Currently, its two ships visit the Caribbean, the Bahamas and Mexico from Tampa and Palm Beach, Fla. A third ship will launch in early 2027 from Miami. Discounted four-night sailings to the Bahamas start at $149 a person during the sale, which runs through Nov. 29.

Until Dec. 1, the luxury cruise line Explora Journeys is offering up to 30 percent off itineraries with a 5 percent deposit at the time of reservation. Travelers who prepay in full can get up to 40 percent off. Among many Caribbean and Mediterranean cruises, the sale covers an 11-night sailing between Barcelona and Athens in March marked down to $5,430 a person from $9,050 when prepaid.

Uniworld Boutique River Cruises is offering half off a companion fare in a shared cabin on select 2027 departures. Running Nov. 17 to Dec. 18, the sale covers cruises including a 12-day trip between Paris and Prague aboard the new ship S.S. Audrey launching next year. The fare normally starts at $4,349 a person in July; the sale would bring the price to about $3,260.

Ski country lodges are doing their part to tame expenses.

Limelight Hotels in Aspen and Snowmass, Colo., and Ketchum near Sun Valley, Idaho, will be offering 40 percent off stays of four nights or more on select dates from January through April. Locations in Mammoth, Calif., and Denver and Boulder, Colo., will offer up to 30 percent off stays of three nights or more.

Look for midweek and March stays for best availability. Rates start at $357 a night in Ketchum before the discount.

On Nov. 30, High Peaks Resort in Lake Placid, N.Y., and Topnotch Resort in Stowe, Vt., will offer a total of 700 room nights at $100 each before taxes and fees, a great savings on accommodations that often command $450 or more. The deal is good for travel between Dec. 1 and March 31. Email subscribers get early access to the sale.

When it comes to lift tickets, Sun Valley Resort will offer three days of skiing for $399 during its sale Nov. 17 to Dec. 1. Blackout dates cover the winter holidays and spring break, but the deal saves $468 over peak window rates.

A number of tour companies have discounts on trips abroad.

item.title: Wall Street Moved Into Insurance. Can State Regulators Keep Up?
item.description:
It was just over a year ago that insurance regulators in Delaware found no significant issues at two life insurers controlled by Mark Walter, a Wall Street billionaire and owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Months later, federal prosecutors started to come to a different conclusion. They collected evidence that those two insurers, Delaware Life and Clear Spring Life, had misclassified billions of dollars in investments with companies affiliated with other parts of Mr. Walter’s vast financial and sports empire, funneling customer money into potentially riskier investments.

Now, prosecutors and securities regulators are trying to determine whether Mr. Walter’s companies broke laws along the way. Amid the scrutiny, he has been selling his stakes in the L.A. Lakers and the British soccer team Chelsea FC, and his two insurers have announced a plan to reduce the level of affiliated investments.

The investigation has analysts, industry executives and lawmakers sorting out another issue: How did the misclassified investments go undetected by Delaware’s insurance examiners?

The answer is crucial because the nation’s 700 life insurers are regulated at the state level. The potential failings in Delaware, where state regulators oversee dozens of life insurers, call into question whether states can keep pace with Wall Street’s growing role in the insurance business.

Ever since the financial crisis of nearly two decades ago, life insurers have forged partnerships with Wall Street as way to expand their businesses. More than 100 of the nation’s life insurance firms are controlled by or linked to a deep-pocketed private equity firm or investment firm. Some of these insurers have begun plowing billions of dollars from customer premiums into the debt being used to finance the construction of A.I. data centers.

Questions about the oversight of those relationships could gather steam in the coming year with Democrats’ taking control of Congress. They are expected to push for stricter financial regulation.

“It’s definitely a miss and they appear to have been asleep at the wheel,” Nick Nemeth, a private investor, said of regulators in Delaware.

Mr. Nemeth has been analyzing insurance filings from Mr. Walter’s companies for other investors and said regulators missed “one of the biggest, boldest numbers you would want to look at in the filings for potential conflicts of interest.”

A spokeswoman for the Delaware insurance regulators declined to comment. The regulators have said in their reports on the insurers that their examination relied partly on work done in 2023 by KPMG, which audits financial filings for both insurers, to look for “current and prospective risks.”

A KPMG spokesman said the firm’s audits were performed “in accordance with the professional standards.

Representatives for Mr. Walter’s holding company, TWG Global, which includes the insurers, sports teams and his interest in the Guggenheim investment firm, declined to comment for this article.

When an insurer invests in a deal with an affiliate, it raises the prospect that these transactions are not fully independent. Another concern is whether a life insurer with a high concentration of affiliated investments is being pushed into riskier assets, said Trace Dodge, a senior vice president at Capstone, a regulatory consulting firm.

For years, Delaware Life, the larger of the two insurers, reported in its financial filings that its investments in affiliated businesses were running at roughly half the industry average of 7 percent. But in June, in the face of a federal investigation, the two insurers disclosed that the firms had collectively underreported the dollar value of investments with businesses associated with TWG Global entities by some $21 billion. Overnight, the dollar value of investments that Delaware Life had made with affiliated businesses rose to about 42 percent of the insurer’s investable assets from a relatively low 3 percent.

The primary mission of an insurance regulator is to make sure a life insurer is making sound investments and has the ability to cover customer claims. Industry analysts said Delaware regulators should have raised more questions about the seemingly low-level of affiliated investments that Mr. Walter’s insurers had been reporting when doing their examinations.

“For years, I avoided criticizing the state regulators,” said Tom Gober, who runs his own forensic accounting firm and has long studied the insurance business. “But it is clear that throughout the private-equity-controlled life and annuity industry, affiliated investments have surged significantly.”

Mr. Nemeth, the private investor and consultant, conducted an analysis of Delaware Life and Clear Spring after the firms reclassified hundreds of investments as affiliated ones. His analysis showed that the two insurers had put money into bonds and loans to the Dodgers, the television company that broadcast Dodgers games and Guggenheim financial products.

He also found loans to dozens of obscurely-named limited liability companies — some of which bore the names of streets in Chicago — near the offices of TWG Global and Guggenheim.

Part of the problem is the business of regulating the nation’s life insurance firms is a fragmented one — making it difficult for any single regulator to get the full picture of the insurance industry landscape. Each state regulator acts independently, and there are no uniform laws. Some insurance commissioners are appointed and others are elected like in Delaware.

Trinidad Navarro, Delaware’s insurance commissioner was first elected into office in 2016 and has since been re-elected twice. Before becoming insurance commissioner, Mr. Navarro was a police officer and a sheriff in New Castle County, Del.

“Regulators have limited bandwidth,” said Tom Baker, an insurance law expert and professor at University of Pennsylvania Carey School of Law. “They aren’t going to check everything.”

In recent years, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, an organization that recommends standards to regulators, has advised its members to require insurers to provide more information about its investments in affiliated and related parties. But the association has no enforcement power, and its recommendations are not binding.

The regulatory missteps related to Mr. Walter’s insurers have prompted calls for change even among the industry’s biggest players.

At a recent banking conference, Marc Rowan, chief executive of Apollo Global Management, the private equity and investment management firm that helped pioneer Wall Street’s move into insurance, said he worried the investigation would lead to a “loss of trust.” He said the situation should be “a wake-up moment for the U.S. regulatory system.”

An Apollo subsidiary, the life and annuity insurer Athene, has roughly $52 billion invested in affiliated transactions, which includes financing deals Apollo has done for other companies. That works out to about 18 percent of the insurer’s investable assets — more than twice the 7 percent industry average.

Other Wall Street-backed insurers have a higher percentage of affiliated investments.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, and a longtime critic of the private equity industry, has said more robust regulation may be needed. She sent a letter in September to the insurance commission association seeking more information about steps that regulators are taking to monitor Wall Street-controlled insurers.

“Wall Street is exploiting gaps in our patchwork of state regulation to enrich itself on Americans’ insurance premiums,” Ms. Warren, who is likely to become the committee’s new chair next year, said in a statement. “We need stronger federal and state standards to close the gaps, rein in private credit and protect families’ savings and retirements from blowing up.”

Kitty Bennett and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Trump’s Plan for A.I. Supremacy Fuels Resistance in the Philippines
item.description:
In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that American officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub.

He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a new initiative called Pax Silica.

Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there?

Months later, he says he has few answers.

“I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez said in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.”

Last December, the United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence.

Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to “Pax Americana,” the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II.

The significance of Pax Silica, which 26 signatories have joined, has become heightened after revelations that Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence, exposing the growing geopolitical stakes of the global A.I. race.

In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce.

More than 70 organizations formed the Network Opposed to Pax Silica. Farmers, students and activists warn it could drain scarce water and electricity supplies and displace hundreds of Indigenous Ayta people. They plan a demonstration when Mr. Trump is expected to arrive in Manila this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

Beyond fears about A.I., the opposition reflects the Philippines’ complicated relationship with its former colonial ruler. Many Filipinos feel a strong cultural affinity for America. But resentment over exploitation runs deep, as does unease over their government’s increasingly close embrace of Washington.

In February, the Philippines signed a memorandum of understanding giving the United States a “first look” at its critical minerals.

“That is unheard-of in the history of our country,” said Renato Reyes Jr., president of Bayan, a political group opposing foreign intervention.

Two months later, the Philippines announced that it had joined Pax Silica and would build a hub about the size of 3,000 football fields. In July, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. pledged that the project would “bring quality jobs to our people, accelerate our industrial competitiveness, and revitalize our economy.”

Local officials wanted to know at what cost.

In August, Roberto Mallari, the Catholic bishop of Tarlac Province, where the hub is planned, met with Joshua Bingcang, head of the government agency overseeing the project. Mr. Rodriguez and other officials were also there.

They pressed Mr. Bingcang on where its power would come from and how many people would be affected.

Mr. Bingcang said the government was considering rainwater harvesting, a desalination plant and a solar farm. More than 100 farmers could be displaced “in the first phase,” he said. Activists estimate the number could be higher.

Bishop Mallari left unconvinced.

“I started to talk about it in my homilies,” he said. “I was telling the parishioners we should get involved in this because we would be the first to be affected.”

Critics question the hub’s resource demands, who would control it and even what it will be.

Government estimates suggest that the project would require up to 90 million liters of water a day and 3 gigawatts of power. Its water needs would require amounts triple the area’s available supply during the dry season, while its projected power demand would be the equivalent of roughly a fifth of Philippine electricity consumption in 2024.

The estimates have fueled suspicions that a sprawling data center is planned. Philippine officials deny this, calling it a semiconductor manufacturing hub.

The State Department was less definite. A spokesman said whether the project would include data centers “will depend on a number of factors, including environmental and infrastructure studies still to come.”

Mr. Bingcang said the project could generate around $3 billion in annual revenue and create up to 190,000 jobs. More than 50 companies, including the world’s tech titans, had expressed interest, he added.

Senator Erwin Tulfo, a politician from a prominent political family, has demanded more clarity on how the hub would operate and whom it would affect, though he remains enthusiastic about the potential jobs.

“It’s money for the country,” he said.

For Senator Imee Marcos, the president’s sister, the issue is sovereignty.

She provided a draft framework that she said was proposed by the Americans. Under its terms, a private “master tenant” would receive a 99-year lease, while a so-called Pax Silica Court in New York would settle disputes.

Ms. Marcos, a critic of her brother’s closer ties to Washington, said she had no objection to an American-led hub.

“You know that the Filipinos love Americans,” she said. “It’s unrequited love, but yeah, it’s unconditional.”

But she warned that the proposed framework could violate Philippine law and the nation’s Constitution, concerns she raised in the Senate.

The State Department denied this, noting that “the Philippines is not transferring land, territory, or sovereign authority to the United States.”

Giovanni Tapang, a former dean of the College of Science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, said supplying the hub’s water needs could require building dams or diverting rivers, depriving farmers of irrigation.

“If we are going to subordinate the development of the country for the U.S.’s needs, then we’re just replicating all the decades of subservience and neocolonial development,” he said.

The proposed Pax Silica site is about a two-hour drive from Manila, in the New Clark City economic zone.

Near a vast stretch of farmland, a sign announcing the project had been taken down. Water buffaloes roam the area. Just 12 miles away stands the former Clark Air Base, once one of America’s largest overseas military bases.

For the Indigenous Ayta people who live nearby, the threat of displacement is painfully familiar.

About 200 Ayta families live in Manabayucan, a remote village on the edge of the planned hub. The Aytas, among the Philippines’ earliest inhabitants, are also among its poorest.

Many were displaced during the Philippine-American War at the turn of the 20th century as the United States established a fort that became the precursor to Clark Air Base.

After Mount Pinatubo, a nearby volcano, erupted in 1991, many people spent years in government camps, unable to resume farming. That same year, the Philippines forced the Americans out of their military bases. But the land was never returned to the Aytas. It passed to the Philippine government.

Reaching Manabayucan requires a drive along an unpaved road, a river crossing and a hike up a steep hill. The village has no electricity, running water or mobile phone coverage.

The outside world feels far away, but now it is closing in.

Nearby, a bulldozer had dug up an Ayta cemetery in what residents said was the beginning of the Pax Silica project.

Many villagers have never heard of artificial intelligence. They know nothing of the fierce opposition to data centers in the United States.

But they understand what losing their land would mean.

Roby Dalis, an Ayta farmer who cannot read or write, earns $4.70 a day selling banana leaves. He recently joined his first protest, traveling to Manila to march alongside other farmers.

“If they take the land where we live, we will have nowhere to go,” Mr. Dalis said.

The Aytas’ plight has become a rallying cause for the movement against Pax Silica. On a recent Thursday, villagers gathered outside their bamboo huts to hear from Kim Falyao, a youth Indigenous activist.

“We should not be dictated upon by anyone saying, ‘We want to build Pax Silica here, so move out,’" she said, as villagers nodded. “No. We have the right to decide for ourselves and our community.”

A day earlier, an Ayta farmer, Nelson de Guzman, spoke at a protest near the presidential palace in Manila. Students held signs reading: “No to Pax Silica.” Protesters destroyed a painted likeness of Mr. Trump.

Mr. de Guzman stepped up to the microphone.

“We need our land,” he said. “We don’t need Pax Silica, and most importantly, we don’t need the U.S.”

The crowd erupted in cheers.

Jes Aznar contributed reporting.

item.title: How Billions in Safe Insurance Money Is Being Bet on A.I. Debt
item.description:
When Elon Musk needed help financing a large purchase of artificial intelligence chips earlier this year, Wall Street offered an elegant solution.

Mr. Musk and his team of advisers created a financial entity that would borrow billions to buy the chips and then lease them back to xAI, his artificial intelligence effort. This way, xAI wasn’t technically the borrower, which helped make its official debt load look smaller to investors.

To help fund this complicated arrangement, $2.4 billion of the debt was sold to an insurance company called Athene, which manages life insurance policies and annuities for retirees, according to a Moody’s Ratings report.

The deal was part of an increasingly popular playbook: tapping insurance companies, which are historically among the most cautious investors, to make loans to tech titans like Mr. Musk and further fuel the A.I. boom.

The amount of A.I. debt being held by insurance companies has soared this year. U.S. life insurers, including some of the largest like Athene and Corebridge Financial, held $85.2 billion in A.I. debt as of June 30, up 24 percent from six months prior, according to Moody’s.

While this accounts for just 2.1 percent of life insurers’ total debt, their exposure is expected to grow quickly. Life insurers could hold up to $185 billion of A.I. investments by the end of next year, according to Moody’s.

Life insurers owned about 15 percent of A.I. data center debt as of June 30, according to a recent estimate by Barclay’s.

These debt investments carry multiple risks. For one, only a few technology companies, including Nvidia, Meta, Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI, are providing the guarantees for these deals, which concentrates the risk. There are also often ways for tech companies to walk away from these A.I. projects if their development is delayed.

“The life insurance industry is now in effect backing large swaths of the A.I. industry,” said Andrew Granato, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law, who has studied the overlap between private equity and insurers.

“We should all be concerned about this, especially as the debt deals get more opaque,” he added.

Making possible this flood of insurance money into risky A.I. deals are credit rating agencies like Moody’s and S&P Global Ratings. They have blessed this rapidly expanding pool of debt with relatively safe credit ratings, which meet the criteria that insurance firms need to invest in a particular asset.

Much of this activity is being driven by giant Wall Street firms that are affiliated with insurance companies and sometimes help manage their investments. Athene, which bought some of the xAI debt, is a subsidiary of the Wall Street firm Apollo.

“Athene finances what we view as the safest and most defensible parts of the A.I. ecosystem,” an Apollo spokeswoman said in a statement.

SpaceX, which owns xAI, did not respond to a request for comment.

Insurers are attracted to A.I. debt because it is regarded as secure, but still offers market-beating returns. A.I. companies, in turn, have come to view the life insurance industry as crucial to supporting their data center expansions.

Last month, Brannin McBee, a co-founder and chief development officer of the data center company CoreWeave, told The Financial Times that he viewed insurers as an “unlimited” source of capital for future borrowing.

“Like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche,” he said.

His comments spooked CoreWeave’s investors and lenders. Its stock dropped sharply the next day and the price of its bonds fell quickly, too. The bonds of other A.I.-related companies and data center projects have also dropped in recent weeks as investors have become more wary of debt risks.

A spokesman for CoreWeave declined to comment.

One of the lenders loudly voicing concerns is Ares Management, one of the largest private credit firms with $691 billion in assets.

In a recent newsletter, Ares argues that tech giants have found ways to bring insurers into risky debt deals with “two-faced transactions.” The tech companies are creating complex financial entities that are being assigned nearly the same secure credit ratings as the tech companies themselves. But, Ares said, there are fewer guarantees that these entities will repay the debt than if the tech giants had borrowed the money directly.

“Sometimes structural complexity and financial engineering are not used to improve risk, but to hide it,” the firm wrote in the newsletter.

Ares cites Meta’s data center in Richland Parish, La., as a prime example.

Rather than owning the project outright, Meta took only a 20 percent stake while the investment firm Blue Owl owns the rest.

Yet, S&P Global was comfortable enough to rate the project’s $27 billion in debt just one notch below Meta’s strong corporate rating because of guarantees the tech company provided. Those included a $28 billion lease guarantee over 20 years or to find a tenant if Meta walked away.

That rating helped open the door for life insurers, which, according to Moodys, funded $3.4 billion of the deal.

But Meta is not promising to repay the project’s debt investors. In a statement, a Meta spokesperson wrote that “Meta has not guaranteed repayment of the bonds.”

In a statement, a Blue Owl spokesman said: “When institutional investors and insurers buy this debt, they are not taking a hidden risk. They are buying exposure to the contractual obligations of some of the strongest corporate credits in the world.”

In another example, Meta signed a deal in March to procure A.I. computing capacity from CoreWeave in four data centers.

When CoreWeave sought a rating for an $8.5 billion loan tied to these projects, the rating agencies looked at Meta’s strong credit rating rather than CoreWeave’s, which is in junk territory, and gave the deal one of its highest ratings. Insurers were buyers of the CoreWeave projects’ debt also, according to S&P Market Intelligence.

But investors are increasingly questioning whether giant companies like Meta deserve such high ratings.

“These companies are not as safe as they once were,” Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor at Columbia Business School, said. “They’re sort of playing this game where they can pretend like they don’t have these liabilities.”

Meta, for example, has signed $356 billion in leases, including for data centers that it has not yet started. That amount is four times larger than the $84 billion of debt that it reported in its latest quarterly filing. Meta has committed an additional $455 billion in deals to buy chips, other infrastructure and hardware, agreements that it cannot cancel.

Last month, S&P Global announced it had revised its 2027 outlook for Meta’s credit rating to negative from stable, citing the surge in future leases and uncertainty about Meta’s ability to turn A.I. spending into revenue. For now, though, Meta’s rating remains the same.

In an interview, Naveen Sarma, an S&P Global Ratings analyst focused on Meta, said his firm did not consider a future lease commitment as existing debt because Meta does not have to start making the lease payments until it starts using the data center.

The Meta spokesperson said the company “respectfully disagrees” with S&P’s outlook. “We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile,” he said.

Moody’s acknowledged the risk of all the debt accumulating off the tech companies’ books in a recent paper. But the firm does not consider those commitments to be existing debt when rating a company’s credit, a Moody’s spokeswoman said.

As for SpaceX, the company’s auditors determined the money that it intended to borrow off its books earlier this year to buy chips should ultimately be recorded as company debt.

But Mr. Musk and Wall Street continue to find innovative ways to keep borrowing. Earlier this month, Mr. Musk raised $40 billion to finance more A.I. chips through a financial entity that will keep that debt off SpaceX’s books for now.

SpaceX could pull off the deal, Mr. Musk said in a post on X, because “we’re investment grade.”

item.title: Apple Was Late to Video Podcasts. Now It’s Trying to Catch Up.
item.description:
Apple helped turbocharge the rise of podcasts two decades ago, but as video podcasts reshape the industry it’s fallen behind competitors like YouTube and Spotify.

Now it’s playing catch up. On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users even if they don’t pay for Apple’s streaming service and will appear on over 1 billion devices that have the Apple TV app, including Rokus and smart TVs. Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app, where it introduced video nine months ago but has been working to bring some of the biggest shows on board.

“We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.”

Video podcasts have proliferated in the past few years as audio creators adapted their shows to reach consumers spending more time on video platforms like YouTube. The video format has proved attractive to celebrities, including Amy Poehler, Pete Davidson and Food Network’s Ina Garten. And the trend of “clipping” — creating short buzzy video clips from longer shows to post on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram — has encouraged creators to add video to their podcasts.

The popularity of video podcasts, driven by YouTube and Spotify, and newer entrants like Hulu and Netflix, has pushed Apple down in the podcast platform rankings. Spotify passed Apple as the top platform among weekly podcast consumers in the United States at the end of 2022, according to survey data from Edison Research at SSRS. YouTube took over the top spot at the end of 2024. In Edison Research’s third-quarter survey, YouTube remained the most popular, followed by Spotify then Apple Podcasts. Netflix was No. 7.

Many in the industry had long awaited Apple’s move.

“It’s super smart that they’ve done it, but it’s after a lot of people in the space wanted them to make it available,” said Megan Lazovick, a vice president at Edison Research.

Apple’s addition of video to its regular app earlier this year has been encouraging, with overall audiences for top shows that added video growing by more than 20 percent on average. That includes shows like IMO with Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson and the comedy podcast Giggly Squad.

Sam Fragoso, the host of the show Talk Easy, had been “eager” for Apple to add video, saying it had doubled the audience of his show, which is also available on Spotify and YouTube.

“It’s so helpful that people can go on their phones, they see a clip on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter and open the Apple app and now watch it on video,” he said. “People are already on their iPhones and they’re used to watching videos on their phones so it was the next logical step.”

Apple’s history may help it catch up to competitors who were earlier to the video podcast boom.

“I love our YouTube audience but it feels not as intentional on that platform — Apple’s where people know where to find their favorite podcasts,” said Rachel Martin, the host of NPR’s Wild Card.

Her show’s audience has grown by more than 60 percent since Apple introduced video, which she called astonishing in an industry where “sometimes it can feel excruciating and really hard to get just another 100 subscribers.”

In 2005, podcasts were viewed as a way for Apple to sell more iPods, the popular audio player that connected to iTunes. (Tech journalists once compared it to a razor company trying to sell more products by distributing free razor blades.) Today, Apple still seems to view video podcasts as a sweetener for devices, including newer products like its iPhone Duo and the upcoming HomeView tablet.

Mr. Schusser said he envisions a future where people can listen to their favorite podcasts as they move through their day.

More than 35 percent of video podcast consumers actively switch between watching and listening to shows in a given month, Apple’s data shows. Some view it as a sign that video podcasts are the future.

“Everything is TV now, which is a little bit heartbreaking for a lifelong audio person to say,” Ms. Martin of NPR said. “I don’t think this is a flash in the pan.”

item.title: A Classic Car Show From Paris Aims to Turn Heads in Manhattan
item.description:
It began as a humble car gathering in a dilapidated former train station in Paris, where hobbyists scoured for flea-market parts. Fifty years later, Retromobile has grown into a bucket-list destination for car lovers: an indoor colossus of collectible cars, restoration specialists, auctions and art, a market for automobilia and delightful oddities.

In France, the Salon Retromobile is further known for its eclectic, egalitarian spirit, one that organizers worked to translate to its inaugural show outside Paris, at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in Manhattan running Thursday to Sunday.

“Automobiles are in the American blood,” said Gerard Neveu, Retromobile’s chief executive. “And New York is the big stage, so we will begin with a splash.”

The splash includes models from two quintessential New Yorkers. While Jerry Seinfeld drove a Saab 900 on his sitcom, he is also known for owning one of the world’s most historically significant Porsche collections.

Four special cars from the Seinfeld Collection will be among those displayed from roughly 200 exhibitors. These include a revolutionary 1955 Porsche 550 Spyder, the brand’s first purpose-built racecar.

A Gooding Christie’s auction will feature more than 70 motorcycles from Billy Joel’s collection, with proceeds benefiting the Joel Foundation. A 1978 Triumph Bonneville T140 with a painted piano-key gas tank was a gift from Madison Square Garden in honor of Joel’s 150th sold-out show. That Triumph is expected to fetch $10,000 to $15,000.

Adding a few zeros, Gooding Christie’s estimates auction bids of $10 million to $15 million for a 1967 Ferrari 275 GTB/4*S NART Spider first owned by Steve McQueen, one of only 10 ever built.

Car fans got an unexpected preview when Retromobile took over a Manhattan neighborhood for a Cars and Coffee event in October. The streets of SoHo, typically the double-parked province of Ubers, became an early-morning flash mob of charismatic machines. Charles Schoendorf chatted up admirers of his 1946 Lancia Aprilia Barchetta Corsa, a sedan converted into a romantic roadster by the Italian coach builder Riva.

“People were taking pictures by the hundreds,” said Mr. Schoendorf, a Connecticut collector whose Lancia will cross the auction block at the show.

Mr. Schoendorf, who has shown his Lancia at Pebble Beach in California and other major events, hopes this French import can become a permanent addition to the global automotive calendar. “I think everybody in the car world is going to be there, considering the show’s success and reputation in Paris,” he said.

Rather than replicating the Paris event, Mr. Neveu says, this show will foreground America’s automotive culture, in a city that’s often stereotyped as being indifferent or hostile toward cars.

The United States, Mr. Neveu countered, is the world’s leading collector-car market. The New York metro area is the nation’s largest new-car market, with many enthusiasts, racers, restorers and collectors.

“People say to me, ‘Gerard, New York is not a car city,’ but it really is,” he said. He added, “There have always been classic cars, clubs, cruisers, everything.”

Gregor Fisken, who owns Fiskens Fine Historic Cars in London, said New York was ideal for Retromobile, as an international city bursting with energy and well-heeled enthusiasts.

“There’s a lot of dollars in your city, and a lot of people are looking to put money into tangible assets,” Mr. Fisken said. “In a world where some North Korean tyrant can steal your bitcoins, that’s a great thing.”

Mr. Fisken’s consignment sale offerings will include two heroes of American motorsports. After a Ford GT40 handed Ferrari a humiliating defeat by sweeping the Le Mans podium in 1966, as chronicled in the movie “Ford v. Ferrari,” the automaker planned to create 20 street-legal GT40s.

A prototype of the GT40 Mark III toured Neiman Marcus department stores before appearing at the 1967 New York Motor Show. Setting the showroom price at $18,500, four times that of a Corvette, Ford ended up building just seven Mark III GT40s. The original show car, one of four with left-hand drive, will be back in New York, its asking price now in the $8 million range.

Another of Mr. Fisken’s offerings is British to its bones. The 1978 Lotus-Cosworth Type 79 was nicknamed Black Beauty, for its black-and-gold livery from the tobacco sponsor John Player Special. But that famous Lotus made Mario Andretti the second and last American driver to win the Formula 1 championship, in 1978.

“The car is coming from an American collector, and it would be great if it stayed in America,” Mr. Fisken said.

This past January, the event’s 50th anniversary in Paris brought a marvel of French engineering: the last surviving Bugatti Autorail, Ettore Bugatti’s sumptuous, speed-record-setting rail car of the 1930s, one of 88 produced. New York counters with its own mammoth: a newly restored Futurliner, first built by General Motors for the 1939 New York World’s Fair. The streamlined Art Deco buses, topped with acrylic bubble canopies, hauled G.M.’s science-and-tech exhibition, the “Parade of Progress,” throughout North America. A fleet of a dozen Futurliners showcased jet engines, microwave ovens, televisions and other innovations.

One of six special exhibitions will feature exceptional cars from the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Italy. Another gallery navigates the intersection among cars, art and pop culture, with art cars from artists including Damien Hirst and Keith Haring and works from artists including Jean-Michel Basquiat and Zaha Hadid.

Henry Ford’s Model T, the 1953 Corvette and the 1961 Jaguar E-Type are among classics that made U.S. auto-show debuts in New York. Ford unveiled its phenomenal Mustang at the 1964 World’s Fair in Queens. Yet traditional new-car shows, once newsmakers and crowd-pleasers in cities from Los Angeles to Tokyo, have waned, undone in part by internet reveals.

The vintage-car and collecting world is also undergoing change. As older collectors “age out” of the hobby, experts cite an unprecedented shift in generational wealth from boomers to younger people. Whatever their age, car fans reliably gravitate to cars they loved as broke teenagers. A dream car released in 1986 is already 40 years old, so many original owners and admirers are in their 60s or even their 70s. Inevitably, the center of gravity for shows and collectors is shifting from Duesenbergs, Rolls-Royces and other prewar classics toward more-recent models.

Many shows are responding by relaxing old rules and giving younger people what they want. Retromobile, Mr. Neveu said, is aware the show must keep evolving.

To that end, a “Youngtimers Gallery” showcases collectible cars from the 1980s and more recently. Memorable cars from the silver screen are featured in another gallery, including the monstrous Ecto-1 car from “Ghostbusters.” Largely Japanese models of the “Fast & Furious” franchise will be presented by the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles.

“It would be awful if this show came off as snooty and elitist, or if you had to have a lot of bucks to come and appreciate it,” Mr. Fisken said.

Paul Russell, a restoration and preservation specialist in Massachusetts, said people who love cars also love sharing them, no matter their brand or backstory.

“This show is an opportunity to talk to a whole new crowd,” said Mr. Russell, whose company will show five cars at the show, including a spectacular 1938 Talbot-Lago T150-C SS Teardrop Cabriolet, a landmark of Art Deco design from France and one of the world’s most desirable prewar cars. The automotive press popularized its nickname, Goutte d’Eau — a Drop of Water. But even as it approaches its 90th birthday, the Talbot-Lago’s timeless style makes it a born influencer, ready for Instagram.

“An enthusiast who thinks a Lotus is cool can go to Retromobile, and suddenly they’re looking at Talbot-Lagos or Hispano-Suizas,” Mr. Russell said. “And it’s going to blow their mind.”
