item.title: How Sam Bankman-Fried Lost Out on a $35 Billion Jackpot From Anthropic
item.description:
Sam Bankman-Fried, the convicted cryptocurrency fraudster, lives in a 30-person unit at the federal prison in Lompoc, Calif., a barbed-wire compound about a million miles away from his former life as a technology billionaire in the Bahamas.

For the most part, Mr. Bankman-Fried, 34, tries not to think about all the “could-have-beens,” he said on a recent call. But one has become difficult to ignore.

In late 2021, the heyday of his FTX crypto exchange, Mr. Bankman-Fried spent $500 million on a 13.5 percent stake in a little-known artificial intelligence start-up called Anthropic. This week, Anthropic is set for an initial public offering that is expected to value the company at $1.4 trillion, potentially one of the largest Wall Street debuts in history.

At that valuation, Mr. Bankman-Fried’s investment, diluted over several years, would now be worth an eye-watering $35 billion — about the size of FTX’s entire business at its peak.

But the shares are gone. They were tied up in bankruptcy court until 2024, when executives overseeing the scattered remains of FTX sold the Anthropic stake for $1.34 billion — a tiny fraction of its current value.

For Anthropic, the fate of those shares is an odd quirk of history. For Mr. Bankman-Fried, it’s a source of extreme frustration and resentment. Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy.

“There’s no point in obsessing over regrets,” he said. “But it’s certainly something that I’ve spent, despite that, a fair bit of time thinking through.”

In September, Mr. Bankman-Fried submitted the longest of long-shot appeals to the Supreme Court, where he cited the Anthropic investment. He claimed that the judge in his trial had improperly prevented him from arguing that FTX had enough money to repay its users.

But none of his arguments was ever likely to overcome the basic facts of FTX’s collapse, an epic financial fraud that drew instant comparisons to Bernie Madoff’s Ponzi scheme. Mr. Bankman-Fried gave up control of FTX in November 2022, after a run on deposits exposed an $8 billion hole in customer accounts. A year later, he was convicted on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. He had used the missing money to buy luxury real estate, donate to political campaigns and invest in start-ups like Anthropic.

Ultimately, the return on those investments proved irrelevant, as far as guilt and innocence were concerned. In U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, Judge Lewis A. Kaplan memorably compared Mr. Bankman-Fried to a “thief who takes his loot to Las Vegas and successfully bets the stolen money.” He sentenced him to 25 years in prison.

“Mr. Bankman-Fried conveniently skips over the fact that he misappropriated and gambled with customer monies,” John J. Ray III, a corporate turnaround expert who oversaw the bankruptcy, said in a statement. “We are proud of the integrity and impact of the work we have done with our large team of committed professionals.”

A spokeswoman for Anthropic declined to comment.

Before FTX filed for bankruptcy, Mr. Bankman-Fried was worth an estimated $24 billion, giving him tremendous influence in business and politics. His company was one of the world’s largest crypto exchanges, a venue where customers could buy, sell and store digital coins.

Mr. Bankman-Fried was also a leading practitioner of “effective altruism,” a philanthropic movement that focuses on combating threats that might emerge decades or centuries in the future. Like many effective altruists, Mr. Bankman-Fried was concerned about the dangers of out-of-control A.I. long before it became a major talking point in American politics.

Those views aligned him with Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, who moved in the same effective altruist circles. Dr. Amodei started the A.I. company after leaving a rival, OpenAI, in late 2020 amid disagreements over how to make the technology safer.

Mr. Bankman-Fried said he spoke with Dr. Amodei not long after that, when FTX was based in Hong Kong. “I was one degree removed and knew a number of people who knew him,” Mr. Bankman-Fried recalled. Dr. Amodei struck him as “really intelligent, dedicated, very knowledgeable.”

In April 2022, Anthropic announced the investment from Mr. Bankman-Fried and two of his FTX colleagues, drawing little notice at the time.

“We cared about A.I. companies being responsible, and preparing for A.I. to help rather than hurt society,” Mr. Bankman-Fried said on the phone from prison. “Anthropic seemed far more committed to that than the other major companies.”

Then in the fall of 2022, FTX plunged into crisis, exposing a giant theft of customer money. Three weeks later, OpenAI released its ChatGPT chatbot, setting off an A.I. frenzy.

Within a year, Mr. Bankman-Fried had been convicted, while Anthropic was raising billions of dollars from high-profile investors like Amazon. It had recently released a popular chatbot, Claude.

As Anthropic turned into one of Silicon Valley’s hottest start-ups, the fate of Mr. Bankman-Fried’s shares became a subject of intense debate in Delaware bankruptcy court.

When FTX failed, Mr. Bankman-Fried had handed control to Mr. Ray, who had managed the unwinding of Enron. Working with the law firm Sullivan & Cromwell, Mr. Ray set out to raise funds to pay back FTX customers in full. Mr. Bankman-Fried had left a messy assortment of corporate assets, including obscure digital coins, properties in the Bahamas and shares in other companies.

Mr. Ray’s team started looking for buyers. A wide-ranging sale is typical in any corporate bankruptcy, where the job of the estate is to maximize recoveries as efficiently as possible. But some customers wanted FTX to sit on the Anthropic stake for longer.

“I wish they held onto it,” said Sunil Kavuri, an FTX customer who testified at Mr. Bankman-Fried’s sentencing. “I foresaw that it would be one of the most valuable assets.”

It didn’t help that Mr. Ray came across as misinformed about the potential value of the shares. In an interview with the author Michael Lewis, he dismissed the company as “this thing called Anthropic.”

“It’s just a bunch of people with an idea,” Mr. Ray said. “Nothing.”

In the end, FTX sold the Anthropic stake at about $30 per share to a few dozen investors, who paid $1.34 billion, according to court filings. The buyers included a business entity linked to Mubadala, the Emirati investment fund; the nonprofit Ford Foundation; and the trading firm Jane Street, which once employed Mr. Bankman-Fried.

A spokesman for the FTX estate said that the sale of the Anthropic stake was “conducted through a court-supervised process and achieved market-value at the time.”

“Billions of stolen funds were misappropriated and invested, without customer consent,” the spokesman said. “There was no way to know at that time whether those investments would succeed or fail and many did fail.”

Representatives for Jane Street and the Ford Foundation declined to comment. Mubadala did not respond to a request for comment.

A bankruptcy estate has significant leeway to decide when and how to sell its assets. Under the circumstances, FTX’s handling of the Anthropic shares was reasonable, said Lindsey Simon, a professor at Emory University School of Law.

“At the time, there was no news about an I.P.O.,” Professor Simon said. “Now we know that they became extraordinarily valuable. But what if they had turned into nothing?”

In May 2024, the estate announced that FTX’s creditors were set to receive as much as $1.18 for every dollar they lost when the exchange failed — more than a full repayment. But that has not quieted the complaints.

The promised returns were pegged to the value of crypto at the time FTX collapsed, when the market was in a deep slump. If customers held Bitcoin on FTX on the day the company filed for bankruptcy, they would be compensated in line with the coin’s price at that moment — not its current price, which is several times higher.

“It was our money, and we didn’t give him rights to use our money,” Mr. Kavuri said. “It sucks.”

These days, Mr. Bankman-Fried has only limited contact with the outside world. He exchanges messages with a network of journalists, friends and relatives, who have kept him up-to-date on A.I. developments. Mr. Bankman-Fried can access the prison phones for 15 minutes at a time, before each call automatically ends.

Over several conversations this fall, he kept returning to Mr. Ray and the bankruptcy lawyers.

“I’m sure you could’ve come up with a way for them to manage it worse,” he said, “but I can’t think of one off the top of my head.”

Mr. Bankman-Fried was repeating grievances that have been repeatedly rejected in court. But does he ever ponder an alternate universe where FTX didn’t implode and the Anthropic shares made him incredibly wealthy?

“A little bit,” he said, starting to answer. “I try not to spend too much time. …”

Then the call cut out.

Cory Weinberg contributed reporting.

item.title: Doubts Loom Over a van Gogh as Auctions Aim for a $2.8 Billion Week
item.description:
The art market’s grand finale beginning Monday comes with a $2.8 billion forecast — and plenty of drama.

A late-breaking claim by heirs of the Jewish former owner of a van Gogh landscape has challenged a Sotheby’s auction Wednesday of a painting of blossoming chestnut trees, which was expected to sell for about $180 million.

The heirs, in an email to the auction house from their lawyer that was shared with The New York Times, said that the canvas was originally sold under Nazi-era duress in 1936, and that they were “prepared to work toward a fair and just solution.”

The high-stakes clash underscores how heavily the three major auction houses are betting on tradition at the New York fall marquee sales of contemporary and modern art. Counting the van Gogh, they are estimating they will sell about $600 million more than last November, when one collector brought a shimmering Klimt portrait home for over $236 million, making it the second-most expensive painting ever auctioned.

Experts said the new estimates reflected a surge in high-value works and signs of confidence in the buying appetites of the ultrawealthy, despite the potential for rising interest rates and recent stock market wobbles.

“There’s been a lot of wealth created since Covid, and there’s still a tremendous appetite this fall for top-quality material that’s fresh to market,” said Liz Sterling, a partner at the New York- and Palm Beach-based advisory firm Sterling Teel Capital.

Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips have mostly relied on death and debt to fill their marquee auctions, though discretionary selling is on the rise. The offerings include a $120 million portrait by Cézanne from an estate built on Argentine sugar wealth and a $60 million portrait by Picasso from the private collection of Jeff Koons, one of the most famous living artists.

The offerings reinforce the growing divide between the market’s top end and everything underneath. The three houses are now offering 47 lots expected to sell for at least $10 million, up from 29 such lots in last November’s equivalent sales. You can expect more traditional works, like an Edward Hopper sailboat painting and an Alberto Giacometti bronze, each priced around $30 million. Still, the very highest price echelon remains thinner than it was at the market’s recent peak. With the van Gogh, there are only two lots estimated above $100 million, compared with five works that sold above that threshold during the 2022 Christie’s estate sale of the Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen.

“Auctioneers or specialists in the past would have said, ‘It’s our job to lead the market, to not only respond to trends but to direct them,’” said the New York-based adviser Alex Glauber. “This season feels much more reactive than proactive in that regard.”

What are they reacting to? One answer is the sustained retreat from speculation on young artists, who are scarce in the week’s evening auctions. Another is the attraction to brand-name luxury objects, such as Patek Philippe watches or a silver Louis XV soup tureen, by global investors whose fortunes have grown dramatically.

“We’re seeing this flight to blue-chip historical artwork, and some of that has to do with people rotating capital out of investments that have perhaps been wealth-generative but also volatile and uncertain,” said Charles Stewart, Sotheby’s chief executive, referring broadly to turbulence in politics and the financial markets.

As the art market prepares for its biggest sales week of the year, here are five bellwethers to watch.

The Impressionist and modern collection of the Argentine sugar heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier is the crown jewel of this month’s auctions, but closer scrutiny last week revealed a discrepancy potentially worth about $180 million.

The vibrant van Gogh landscape “Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees),” from 1890, could be withdrawn from the auction — or, if the claim is settled before Wednesday, go on to sell for more. Among 12 lots expected to make about $450 million, the trove also contains Paul Cézanne’s “Arlequin” (1888-90), estimated in the region of $120 million.

The disputed van Gogh landscape changed hands multiple times between 1936 and its acquisition by the Blaquier-Arrieta family in 1975. It now hangs in the balance of negotiations between Sotheby’s, the Blaquier-Arrieta estate and the heirs’ lawyers. “While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution,” the auction house said.

Backed by a financial guarantee from Sotheby’s to the consignor, the van Gogh would likely eclipse the Dutch artist’s current auction record of $117.2 million for a landscape sold at Christie’s in 2022, at the Paul Allen sale (about $135 million in today’s dollars).

Painted within four days of his arrival in pastoral Auvers following a year spent in a psychiatric asylum, the verdant chestnut trees against a gathering storm can be read as symbols of the artist’s emotional struggle. Now the composition could equally symbolize the clash over its ownership.

In the late 2000s, as his own market ascended on the sale of balloon-animal sculptures, the artist Jeff Koons went on a buying spree. He scooped up work by artists who inspired him, like Picasso, Manet and the Dutch Golden Age painter Cornelis van Haarlem. Seven of those works are expected to sell for a total of more than $100 million as part of the 20th-century evening sale Tuesday at Christie’s, with Picasso’s passionate canvas “Le Baiser” estimated at $40 million to $60 million.

Although his name doesn’t appear in official materials, Koons is undoubtedly the consignor. “The fact that he owned these only adds to the mystique around the works,” said Jacob King, an art adviser, noting that strong provenance can lead to higher prices even when an artist like Koons doesn’t necessarily want his name associated with a sale.

A person close to the Christie’s deal said that Koons’s motivation for selling the collection was to invest back into his art practice.

Demand for younger artists has fallen sharply since the speculative frenzy peaked five years ago. But the market still anoints a few stars each season.

The name of the moment is Joseph Yaeger, a 40-year-old Montana-based painter of closely cropped and altered film stills. The artist’s use of watercolor on gesso gives his surfaces a pockmarked, crackled quality. Collectors vied for paintings from Yaeger’s show this fall at Gladstone in New York, where advisers said prices ranged from $35,000 to around $200,000.

Experts anticipate his prices at auctions this week — at Phillips on Tuesday and Christie’s on Thursday could go significantly higher. Last month, a dramatically lit painting of a woman’s face by Yaeger sold in London for nearly $855,000 — a 79 percent rise over his previous auction record, set just six months earlier.

“There’s pent-up demand,” the art adviser Benjamin Godsill said. “If you need to have one of these right now, access to capital is easier than access to paintings.”

When the Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama died this year at 97, critics debated whether her commercial success had overshadowed her artistic vision. A market juggernaut, she was one of the few artists (and the only woman) to cross $1 billion in total auction sales, according to the market database ARTDAI.

Can the strength of her market survive doubts about her involvement in late-career works? Kusama’s last public appearance was in 2017, fueling speculation that her studio assistants directed the production of large-scale works, like her pumpkin sculptures. Authorship doubts would typically decrease the valuation of an artwork, but this week’s sales will show whether Kusama is an exception to the rule.

“There hasn’t been a test of Kusama for the late works since she died,” the adviser Wendy Cromwell said.

Klimt was “one of the least prolific of the great modern painters,” said Max Carter, a Christie’s executive.

The artist completed only about 50 landscapes, many of which are owned by museums unlikely to sell. But just a year after three of Klimt’s paintings sold for almost $400 million combined at Sotheby’s, an anonymous seller is hoping to capitalize on the artist’s popularity with “Litzlbergkeller,” an intimate view of Klimt’s beloved lakeside retreat.

David Schrader, a founder of the dealership Pace Di Donna Schrader Galleries, said the demand for premier Klimt works is “certainly deeper and broader than we would have thought two years ago,” spanning the Americas, Europe and Asia. Even if no other bidders emerge, the financial guarantee already made by a third party ensures “Litzlbergkeller” will be among the week’s top sellers.

item.title: As Phillips Scales Back, the ‘Big Two’ Auction Houses Seem to Stand Alone
item.description:
Two works in this week’s marquee auction at Phillips — a loosely brushed group portrait by David Hockney and a roughly hewed limestone head sculpture by Amedeo Modigliani — carry estimates above $10 million. Compare that with what’s on offer at Christie’s and Sotheby’s: a combined 45 lots above that blue-chip threshold.

“One client described us as scrappers and I loved that description,” said Martin Wilson, Phillips’s chief executive. “That is how we put our sales together. We don’t get a ready-made big collection landing in our laps.”

Like Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Phillips has an English pedigree planted in the 18th century, when it managed the estate sales of dead aristocrats. But in recent years, the company seems to have retreated from its centuries of competition with the “Big Two,” leaving some experts in the art market to worry about having to deal with a true duopoly.

In today’s auction market, it’s expensive to sell top material. Auction houses increasingly rely on financial guarantees to win consignments, promising sellers millions of dollars before the auctioneer even picks up the gavel. They fly paintings to Paris, Taipei and Hong Kong, recruit celebrity bartenders to work their parties, and hire star architects to design their salesrooms.

Wilson, who joined Phillips as a lawyer in 2018 and became chief executive in 2024, objected to the idea that the company was shying away from this kind of competition. But, he said, Phillips no longer intended to grow at all costs. “You start with growth being the priority over profitability. We had reached that point in growth where we had credibility,” he said, and it was “time really to look at profitability.”

The pivot has discouraged salespeople who were drawn to Phillips by the prospect of building a viable competitor. “The company that I put 10 years of my life into, and had a lot of fun and success doing so, is now a very different beast,” said Jonathan Crockett, who resigned as chairman of Phillips Asia in September. “The strategy no longer resonated with me.”

It wasn’t always this way.

Four years ago, Phillips looked poised to challenge its bigger rivals. The company was operating out of a sleek new space and the bidding was frothy. Among the spring sales: an $85 million painting by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a $20 million blue monochrome by Yves Klein and a $15.7 million sculpture by Alexander Calder. Phillips sold $746 million worth of art and design in 2022 — a record for the company.

Phillips’s nimbleness and rapid expansion made it “the envy of the bigger auction houses,” said Caroline Sayan, chief executive of the art advisory Cadell North America. The company branded itself as a less formal, more youthful alternative to its rivals, with a narrower focus on modern and contemporary art and watches.

Even if the revenue still only accounted for about 7 percent of the industry’s total sales, according to information from ARTDAI, a market database, experts said Phillips had become a wedge between Christie’s and Sotheby’s that increased the bargaining power of consignors. Sellers whose $18 million Joan Mitchell painting might be fifth-billed at the big houses could get star treatment at Phillips.

“The more competition in the auction market, the better it is for consignors,” said Thomas Danziger, a lawyer who often represents art sellers. “To have a third leg of the stool is important to any healthy market, especially the art market. Two-legged stools never do as well.”

The owners of Mercury Group, one of Russia’s largest luxury goods conglomerates, completed their acquisition of Phillips in 2012. The goal was growth. With the support of its owners, the house began to win some trophy lots by offering sellers a guaranteed minimum price better than what Sotheby’s and Christie’s were offering. “It was a quick transformation,” said Cheyenne Westphal, Phillips’s former global chairman.

Total sales more than doubled between 2014 and 2018, outpacing the growth of its rivals, according to ARTDAI.

During the pandemic, Phillips benefited from a market frenzy around the young artists that it specialized in selling. And the company largely evaded scrutiny for its connection to Russian elites after the country’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, releasing a statement opposing the war and donating $7.7 million to the Ukrainian Red Cross. “There was a question about ‘Where does Phillips stand,’ and the moment we made that clear, it was resolved,” Wilson said. “I don’t think it has affected us at all.”

But some potential clients still harbored reservations about working with the firm, according to three former executives, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private business matters.

And the Russian owners and Mercury Group founders, Leonid Fridlyand and Leonid Strunin — amid a larger contraction in the art market — became more reluctant to invest the hundreds of millions of dollars necessary to win major collections, the former executives said. For example, Phillips retreated from a yearslong effort to secure a $922 million collection from the divorcing billionaires Harry and Linda Macklowe, according to four former executives. Sotheby’s won the trove, which became the most valuable collection sold at auction at the time.

Phillips’s ownership further soured on guarantees after its sale of the Triton Collection, a group of Cubist and Expressionist paintings the house had stretched to secure in 2023, did not deliver the results it hoped for, according to three former executives. (A Phillips spokeswoman, Jaime Israni, denied that the sale, which generated $84.7 million, was disappointing to the owners.)

“In the high-stakes auction market today, the name of the game in attracting collections and major works of art is clearly the house guarantee,” Danziger said. “Sotheby’s and Christie’s have the risk tolerance to place big bets and win these consignments. Phillips, not so much.”

Wilson disputed that the owners had reined in their support. “They have reiterated their unwavering commitment to Phillips, remaining optimistic about the future and success of the company,” he said.

Some former staff disagreed with what they saw as a shift toward what the industry calls the “middle market”: art between $50,000 and $500,000, and most members of Phillips’s leadership team in 2020 are no longer with the company. “The exciting part of being at an auction house is selling those big-ticket items,” Crockett said.

While Christie’s and Sotheby’s have cornered the high end, there is also growing competition in the middle market and other categories that Phillips sells, like jewelry and prints.

Bonhams topped Phillips in reported sales last year, making $43 million more than its competitor, while also opening a splashy new headquarters a few blocks uptown on a stretch of Manhattan known as Billionaire’s Row. Heritage Auctions capitalized on the growing appetite for collectibles — from Superman comics to the “Rosebud” sled from “Citizen Kane” — to reach a record $2.2 billion in sales in 2025.

Wilson said that Phillips remained committed to the market’s high end, pointing to this week’s Modigliani as an example. (To win the consignment, Phillips rapidly secured a buyer to guarantee the seller a minimum price for the sculpture, which carries an estimate of $28 million to $35 million.) While the margins are better in the middle market than at the top level, “you have to deal with both if you’re an auction house,” Wilson said.

Wilson is bullish on Phillips’s ability to grow its business without spending too much along the way. The house held its first modern and contemporary art auction in Paris in October and, thanks in part to its rare Modigliani sculpture, the high estimate for this week’s evening sale in New York is up almost 45 percent from last year. Wilson says the house intends to continue investing in watches, where it leads the industry: This month in Geneva, Phillips staged the most lucrative watch auction in history, bringing in $112.3 million.

But some experts say that luxury objects — which have also been a growing focus of Sotheby’s and Christie’s — cannot replace the revenue generated by art. “The revenue of one top day sale painting is maybe 50 watches,” Sayan said.

The next few years will determine what kind of business Phillips wants to become.

“We’ve got massive ambition and at the end of the day we want to compete at the highest level we can,” Wilson says. “But we are the organization we are and we’re going to grow using the tools at our disposal.”

item.title: Is Jensen Huang Plotting a Comeback?
item.description:
Andrew here. The Jensen Huang–Nvidia tale has escalated into a high-stakes tug of war.

On one side, Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley figures are mounting a pressure campaign to reinstate Huang as C.E.O. But Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a “dramatic shake-up” and an outside replacement, citing concerns that Nvidia may have bypassed export laws by selling chips to Chinese-linked intermediaries. (Adding a new wrinkle, Megaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the scandal, left the firm in August 2025.)

What happens next is anyone’s guess. The former Nvidia chief is expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks. But the ultimate showdown may happen overseas: President Trump is heading to China to meet President Xi Jinping, where this topic is almost certain to come up. Or is it? More below.

It’s been four days since Jensen Huang resigned as the C.E.O. of Nvidia, after news reports said he had an affair with Alice Huang, the data center executive U.S. intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy. (He also had an affair with a direct subordinate, The Times has reported.)

Now, some of Silicon Valley’s biggest heavyweights want to reinstate Huang, even as some Trump administration officials called for new blood atop the chip maker at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.

Yet there are signs that President Trump himself may not raise the issue even as he prepares to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s top leader.

Huang is reportedly on board with efforts to bring him back, The Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources. Ever since he resigned, many in Silicon Valley have wondered whether he would lead a comeback, much as Sam Altman did after briefly being ousted from OpenAI nearly three years ago.

A Who’s Who of the tech world has rallied around Huang, including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney of Epic Games.

Musk argued over the weekend on social media that many of Nvidia’s crucial supply chain agreements were “a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract” — and that without him, “at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Other executives have pointed to comments by Attorney General Todd Blanche last week saying that the Justice Department hadn’t concluded that Alice Huang was a spy.

What’s at stake:

Huang’s interim replacement, Colette Kress, is widely expected to rein in the huge subsidies Nvidia had offered throughout the A.I. ecosystem, after having questioned them while C.F.O. of the company.

Some tech executives worry that Huang’s departure removed an influential supporter of relaxed regulations on A.I. and of open A.I. models, as opposed to closed ones from OpenAI, Anthropic and others.

But major figures like Scott Bessent reiterated that Huang had to go. Bessent, the Treasury secretary, publicly questioned Nvidia’s sales of chips to companies like Megaspeed that are accused of smuggling processors to China: On Fox News, he asked whether the company pursued “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings.”

He added that the company needed a “dramatic shake-up” — widely interpreted as a demand for an external candidate for C.E.O.

The Trump factor: The president, who had a close bond with Huang, so far has suggested that he doesn’t intend to bring up the U.S. intelligence findings about Huang and Alice Huang with Xi when the two meet this week on the sidelines of the APEC conference in Shenzhen, China. (Beijing has called the findings “groundless smears and slanders.”)

In fact, The Wall Street Journal reports, the Trump administration still plans to name Nvidia as an A.I. “national champion,” putting it in line to get expedited approval for chip exports and tap federal financing. The program is overseen by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department Bessent publicly rebuked for failing to blacklist Megaspeed.

Travelers in the U.S. brace for more flight delays. Airport disruptions looked set to ease, but more than 1,200 flights were delayed or canceled as of 7 a.m. Eastern, according to FlightAware. Shares of L3Harris Technologies, which operates infrastructure the Federal Aviation Administration uses, fell in premarket trading after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy vowed to investigate whether the company’s work caused the nationwide ground stop on Friday. Investigators focused on a router in Arkansas installed by L3Harris and warned that more failures could occur.

Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine’s access to Starshield is being affected again. Ukraine’s president said the country’s military was experiencing another throttling of the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian drone attacks. Democrats and Republicans in Congress have vowed to investigate Kyiv’s accusations. The Pentagon said on Friday that it was looking into the matter.

It’s a big week for Wall Street and geopolitics. Major companies are reporting quarterly results, including Disney, Home Depot and Nvidia on Tuesday, and Walmart and Alibaba on Thursday. Also on Thursday, President Trump is slated to meet with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir Putin of Russia at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China (where the economy is showing more signs of a slowdown).

The sell-off in cryptocurrencies is gaining momentum, and Bitcoin bulls are bracing for more trouble before Anthropic’s highly anticipated trading debut this week.

Bitcoin was trading below $65,000 on Monday, extending a slump that has wiped out more than $400 billion in market value since the hack last month of Binance, a major crypto exchange. The F.B.I. said North Korea was responsible for the heist, in which some $6 billion in digital currency was stolen.

What’s behind the downturn? Market watchers point to multiple factors, including rising interest rates and a wider investor rotation out of digital currencies and into the next hot thing — artificial intelligence.

“AI sucked the air out of crypto,” Kevin O’Leary, the entrepreneur and TV personality from “Shark Tank,” wrote on social media over the weekend. “For a while, crypto was the hot thing to invest in, then it wasn’t.”

The upcoming Anthropic I.P.O. and a flood of investors unwinding their bets on crypto-focused exchange-traded funds may be contributing to the wider decline, Changpeng Zhao, a founder of Binance, wrote Sunday on social media. (Unlike O’Leary, Zhao struck a bullish outlook for crypto.)

Analysts have been warning about an A.I. effect on crypto for months. They see mega-listings by A.I. giants, including Anthropic and possibly OpenAI next year, potentially accelerating crypto’s downward trend. DealBook reported this in June before SpaceX’s market debut, when the buzz for A.I. stocks began to deflect attention away from crypto chatter on investor message boards.

A big question on Wall Street is whether investors will now sell crypto assets to snatch up Anthropic shares. Reuters and Bloomberg report, citing unnamed sources, that investor demand for Anthropic shares is robust. The A.I. colossus is set to price its shares on Wednesday before a trading debut on Thursday.

What could revive crypto’s fortunes? Digital asset prices did rebound in August on hopes of a legislative victory for the Clarity Act, a business-friendly bill that the industry put significant lobbying muscle behind. But that effort stalled in the Senate weeks later, with Democrats blocking it largely over concerns about the Trump family’s crypto gains.

Democrats’ resounding midterm election victory looks set to usher in tighter legislative controls on the industry — another ominous sign for crypto bulls and for the Trump family’s business ventures in this area.

Picture of the day

SpaceX made history on Saturday when the company caught the upper stage of a returning Starship rocket, using mechanical “chopsticks” arms attached to its launch tower in Texas. (SpaceX, Elon Musk’s company, has caught the bottom section, the Super Heavy booster, before.)

The achievement underscores Musk’s lead in the space race — especially after a Vulcan rocket from United Launch Alliance, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed ​shortly after liftoff on Sunday. The mishap destroyed a payload of 40 satellites from Amazon’s Leo internet network, a competitor to Musk’s Starlink whose customers include Delta Air Lines and AT&T.

The artificial intelligence buildout is expected to cost trillions of dollars and is already testing the limits of the financial markets.

To fund this immense undertaking, tech titans and Wall Street are getting creative. And increasingly, they’re turning to one of the few pools of capital large enough to provide such a gargantuan sum: insurance companies.

The result has left insurers, historically among the most cautious investors, holding billions in A.I. debt that carries multiple risks, Niko Gallogly and Maureen Farrell report for The Times.

Insurers’ A.I. investments have soared this year. U.S. life insurance companies, including industry leaders like Corebridge Financial and Athene, held $85.2 billion in A.I. debt as of June 30, up 24 percent from six months before, according to Moody’s.

Moody’s estimates that life insurers could hold up to $185 billion of A.I. debt by the end of next year.

“We should all be concerned about this, especially as the debt deals get more opaque,” said Andrew Granato, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law, who has studied the overlap between private equity and insurers.

They’re highly concentrated bets. A handful of companies, including Alphabet, Anthropic, Meta, Nvidia and OpenAI, largely back the A.I. debt, concentrating the exposure for the insurance companies.

And there are growing questions about whether the state regulators overseeing U.S. life insurers can keep up with the growth of these deals.

Big Tech has targeted insurance money. Large technology companies have found ways to lure insurers into risky debt deals with “two-faced transactions” that appear safer than they are, according to a recent newsletter by the investment giant Ares Management.

To lower their own risk, Silicon Valley giants are pushing debt off their balance sheets by creating complex financial entities that are being assigned nearly the same secure credit ratings as the tech companies themselves.

But, Ares said, there are fewer guarantees that these entities will repay the debt than if the tech giants had borrowed the money directly.

How it works: Ares cites Meta’s Hyperion data center in Richland Parish, La., as a prime example. Rather than owning the project outright, Meta took a 20 percent stake, while the investment firm Blue Owl owns the rest.

S&P Global was comfortable enough with the financing to rate the project’s $27 billion in debt just one notch below Meta’s strong corporate rating because of guarantees that Mark Zuckerberg’s company provided. That rating helped open the door for life insurers, which, according to Moody’s, funded $3.4 billion of the deal.

But Meta is not promising to fully back the debt. In a statement, a Meta spokesman wrote, “Meta has not guaranteed repayment of the bonds.”

Deals

Sound Ventures, a venture capital firm founded by Guy Oseary, Madonna’s manager, and the actor Ashton Kutcher, has reportedly built a stake in Anthropic worth $7 billion. (Bloomberg)

Diamondback Energy, the big U.S. shale oil producer, is reportedly working on a deal to buy a drilling portfolio in Texas from Double Eagle for about $5 billion. (FT)

“SpaceX’s S&P 500 Bid Gets New Life as Musk Pitches Tesla Merger” (Bloomberg)

Technology and artificial intelligence

Controversy above: People complain that Amazon delivery drones that sound like flying leaf blowers are “stealing the sky,” while scientists warn that space data centers could end stargazing as we know it. (WSJ, Axios)

“U.S. and allies sign accord to protect A.I. supply chains from China” (FT)

Best of the rest

Warren Buffett donated about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to philanthropies overseen by his children. (CNBC)

Wanted: wealth advisers to help newly rich artificial intelligence techies give away their money. (WSJ)

“The rise and fall of LIV Golf: How a $5 billion illusion met reality” (The Athletic)

item.title: Robert Pattinson Named as the Next James Bond
item.description:
After seven years of rumors, wish lists and wild guesses, Hollywood’s most feverishly followed casting search is over: Amazon MGM Studios has chosen Robert Pattinson to play James Bond.

Pattinson, the 40-year-old English actor, will become the seventh man to play 007 in the official 25-film series. Pattinson is known for blockbusters like “Twilight,” “The Batman” and, most recently, “The Odyssey.”

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson said in a statement.

He succeeds Daniel Craig, who announced in 2019 that he would depart the role. Craig’s decision set off a frenzy of speculation among Bond enthusiasts, bookmakers and the British tabloids. Who could be trusted to step into the multibillion-dollar franchise? What kind of Bond would click with a new generation? Should Bond be Black? Or female?

At various points, the supposed candidates included Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Hardy, Regé-Jean Page, Tom Holland, Jacob Elordi and Theo James.

Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

James Bond is one of the most coveted — and unforgiving — roles in moviedom. When Craig was cast in 2005, taking over from Pierce Brosnan, detractors complained that he was too blond, too short and insufficiently suave. Carping fans have long been part of the Bond tradition, but the internet gave them a new megaphone. Craig’s “fleshy” ears and “potato” face were mocked on message boards. One group even created a protest website, CraigNotBond.com.

Craig went on to become one of the most celebrated Bonds, but playing a superspy with a license to kill took a physical toll. Over five films, he suffered injuries to his shoulder, calves, knee and ankle while shooting action sequences, at one point questioning whether he could continue.

The character also comes with a complicated cultural legacy, including what Helen Mirren has called his “profound sexism.” Nor is Bond’s appearance the only thing purists obsess over. Even minor adjustments to his martini order can be treated as grounds for an international incident: The product-placement Heineken he drank in “Skyfall” did not go down smoothly.

But this is no ordinary 007 handoff.

Amazon is attempting to reinvigorate a series that has been without a new movie since 2021, with the hiatus on track to become the longest in Bond history. In the franchise’s absence, a new generation of moviegoers has come of age with little attachment to the glamorous British spy, gravitating instead toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is also proceeding without the Broccoli family, whose expert stewardship of the franchise — over six decades — turned it into one of the most valuable properties in Hollywood history.

Amazon acquired a 50 percent stake in the Bond movies as part of its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM in 2022. Barbara Broccoli and her half brother, Michael G. Wilson, retained ownership of the rest — along with final say over creative decisions. In 2025, after years of behind-the-scenes tensions over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe, the tech giant wrested creative control from Broccoli and Wilson.

Albert “Cubby” Broccoli, her father and his stepfather, first brought James Bond to the big screen with “Dr. No” in 1962. The official series has since generated nearly $7 billion in domestic ticket sales alone, after adjusting for inflation. Some longtime fans have worried that the films will become more corporate and American in style, losing their distinctly British character. With so much at stake, Amazon recruited Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman who has become one of Hollywood’s most successful producers. David Heyman, the producing force behind all eight “Harry Potter” movies, is also helping to chart Bond’s future.

The 26th Bond film — not counting two made outside the official series, “Casino Royale” (1967) and “Never Say Never Again” (1983) — will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, whose credits include the Oscar-nominated “Dune” movies. Steven Knight, creator of the crime drama “Peaky Blinders,” is writing the screenplay. It’s an original story. “Casino Royale” in 2006 was the last Bond movie based substantially on an Ian Fleming novel. There are no more to adapt.

A release date has not been announced. Bond movies typically require six to seven months of filming alone, making a theatrical debut before 2028 unlikely.

Tess Felder contributed reporting from London.

item.title: Elon Musk Dreams of a Conglomerate in Move Toward Technological Supremacy
item.description:
No one could accuse Elon Musk of thinking small. And the vision he described last month of merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla is characteristically ambitious: a digital conglomerate of unprecedented scale, spanning rockets, satellites, electric cars, robots and social media.

Mr. Musk is not alone as a digital-age corporate empire builder. Other tech giants are also now sprawling, multi-industry enterprises.

Alphabet’s businesses range well beyond Google search and cloud computing to include video streaming, self-driving cars, drone delivery service and drug development. Amazon has e-commerce, cloud computing, video streaming, a movie studio, robots, warehouses and delivery services.

But a SpaceX-Tesla merger would eclipse the others in its striking array of different businesses, forming a mega-conglomerate worth about $3.5 trillion.

Conglomerates of the past were typically driven by purely financial considerations, like the 1960s merger frenzy on Wall Street, or to diversify a company in order to make it better able to weather economic cycles and international competition, like General Electric.

But today’s conglomerate impulse has a different source — a drive for technological supremacy by broadening a corporation’s market reach and gaining an upper hand in the global A.I. race.

“These big companies are trying to deploy digital technologies, and increasingly artificial intelligence, across industries,” said David Yoffie, a professor at the Harvard Business School.

Mr. Musk acknowledged that the logic of a SpaceX-Tesla merger was a corporate move to seize the A.I. moment. The A.I. businesses at SpaceX include its Grok chatbot and A.I. software models, its data center-building unit and its Cursor A.I. coding assistant. Tesla would bring self-driving cars, robotaxis, humanoid robots and A.I. chip design.

During a SpaceX investor call last month, when Mr. Musk disclosed the two companies were exploring a merger, he said there was “a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” the stage at which A.I. surpasses human intelligence.

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest person, is chief executive and the largest shareholder of both companies. So special committees of independent directors at both companies will weigh whether to go ahead.

Corporate conglomerates in America have a rich, colorful and mostly disappointing history. The 1960s saw an explosion of deal making to build the fast-rising conglomerates of their day like ITT Corporation, Litton Industries, Gulf and Western Industries and Ling-Temco-Vought.

These companies were agglomerations of unrelated businesses. ITT (International Telephone and Telegraph) began as an communications company operating outside the United States, but it came to own Avis rental cars, Levitt home builders, Sheraton hotels, Scott’s fertilizer, Wonder Bread and Morton’s frozen foods, among others.

Wall Street was hot. So the currency of acquisition — the buying company’s stock price — was inflated. Debt was cheap and the accounting was creative.

Sleight-of-hand financial deals were the order of the day. One of its foremost practitioners was James Ling — “Jimmy Ling, the merger king.” He started an electrical contracting business in Dallas. Over the years, in deal after deal, he acquired companies in steel manufacturing, meatpacking, car rentals, military aircraft, car rentals, an airline and resorts. At its peak in 1969, LTV, as the company was known, ranked 14th in the Fortune 500.

But the 1960s bull market on Wall Street ended abruptly as inflation rose. LTV’s stock price plummeted, Ling was ousted and LTV went through a string of bankruptcies.

Still, even after the 1960s conglomerate bubble, there were multi-industry companies that thrived. The leading example grew out of the power generators to lightbulbs conglomerate formed in 1892, when Thomas Edison’s Edison General Electric Company merged with another company.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, General Electric enjoyed two decades of prosperity under the leadership of Jack Welch. G.E.’s revenue jumped nearly fivefold, to $130 billion, during Mr. Welch’s tenure. The value of its shares on the stock market soared from $14 billion to more than $410 billion, making G.E. one of the most valuable companies in the world.

In 2000, Fortune magazine named Mr. Welch the “Manager of the Century”

G.E. seemed proof that a well-run industrial conglomerate could enjoy the advantages of size, funding, shared research and expertise. Like the digital giants of today, G.E. executives spoke of critical industrial technologies — physics and materials science — that could be applied to different industries. A gas turbine power generator, they explained, was essentially a big jet engine bolted to the ground.

But under Mr. Welch, G.E. diversified beyond industrial businesses into finance and commercial real estate. G.E.’s leaders viewed the company’s greatest asset as its management excellence, which they figured could be applied to any business. The money to be made on Wall Street looked easy compared to manufacturing.

For years, the buildup of that business paid off. The company’s finance arm, GE Capital, accounted for up to half of corporate profits in some years and became the largest nonbank financial institution in America. But the 2008 financial crisis hit the division hard.

In 2021, G.E. announced it was splitting into three companies: GE Aerospace, for jet engines; GE Vernova, for power generators and wind power; and GE Healthcare, for medical imaging equipment. The breakup was completed in 2024, as the once-iconic American corporate behemoth bowed to changing times and fortunes.

Studies of conglomerates over the years have found that the stock market value of the combined corporation is typically worth 10 to 15 percent less than if the businesses were stand-alone companies, known as the conglomerate discount. The benefits of combining businesses — the much-praised “synergies” — are overwhelmed by the complexity of managing varied operations and the difficulty of getting a clear picture of the performance of individual businesses.

Skeptics of a SpaceX-Tesla deal point to those challenges. “Shareholders can already own both companies, and this transaction would have all the drawbacks of a conglomerate,” said Baruch Lev, a professor emeritus of accounting and finance at New York University’s Stern School of Business.

Mr. Musk is an experienced corporate acquirer and he has proved skeptics wrong in the past, though a SpaceX-Tesla tie-up would be his largest deal by far. But the merger is not just about corporate size, it is a bet on the “A.I. synergies” that Mr. Musk hopes will result. Much will depend on how much shared A.I. technology and knowledge can be spread across the varied businesses, yielding cost savings and competitive gains, better products and services.

Some analysts say an A.I. conglomerate may well enjoy advantages as the technology is increasingly widely adopted. A combined SpaceX and Tesla, they say, will have greater power to develop, buy and build the technology and deploy it across industry after industry.

They cite the increasing collaboration already between SpaceX and Tesla, led by the giant SpaceX computer chip plant in Texas, announced earlier this year, which will cost at least $55 billion and in total spending could reach $119 billion. Both companies will use the chips manufactured in Texas, with Tesla-designed semiconductors made there as well.

“In this A.I. economy, where computing capacity rules the world, putting SpaceX and Tesla together makes a lot of sense,” said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, an investment research firm.

item.title: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
item.description:
Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: build a sports car that can fly.

Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.

This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.

This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.

The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest man has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.

For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

“It’s unusual because they have a common C.E.O. who is one of the wealthiest people on the planet,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management. “There’s nothing like this that’s happened. Even in the days of John D. Rockefeller, you didn’t have this kind of consolidation of wealth and power.”

Representatives for Tesla and SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The merger will require approval by independent committees from each company, and approval by shareholders.

Mr. Musk has said the companies’ work overlaps closely and he thinks a merger would be a “good idea.” But he has said he will not be a part of any special committee discussions, comparing the decision to “tap dancing through a minefield.”

Mr. Musk has rapidly consolidated his business empire over the past few years. In February, he merged his A.I. start-up, xAI, with SpaceX, bringing in engineers from the rocket company to lead key projects, including xAI’s data center build out and a reorganization of the start-up, according to five people with knowledge of the company. The acquisition took place less than a year after he merged the A.I. start-up with his social media company, X. The combined SpaceX, which went public in June, is valued at $1.89 trillion.

A merger of Tesla, which is valued at $1.54 trillion, and SpaceX would combine the electrical vehicle manufacturer and its solar business with a government contractor with ambitions to send astronauts to Mars. The massive deal would wrap cars, rockets, satellites, data centers and A.I. into one company.

“The synergies are pretty obvious,” said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business. “There’s loads of conflicts of interest. They all get resolved with this merger.”

Some of the existing connections between the companies — most of which are paid for by the companies — have been detailed in contracts and public filings. In the prospectus SpaceX’s initial public offering, the company said it had bought about $890 million in Tesla products since 2023, including Cybertrucks and Megapack batteries to help power the company’s data centers. The filing also detailed how the companies share private jets.

Tesla has incorporated some SpaceX products into its offerings, including adding Grok, an A.I. assistant, as a chat feature in Tesla vehicles and incorporating SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service into its future vehicles. Tesla announced in January it had invested $2 billion in xAI as a part of a larger partnership between the two companies.

But much of the overlap can be traced to staffing.

The two companies have shared some talent for more than a decade. Charlie Kuehmann has served as vice president of materials engineering for both companies since 2015. And earlier this year, Tesla’s vice president of A.I., Ashok Elluswamy, the man responsible for leading Tesla’s self-driving software and work on humanoid robotics, began working simultaneously with SpaceX’s A.I. unit, according to two people with knowledge of his work. About one in 22 SpaceX employees list Tesla as a former employer, and the carmaker is SpaceX’s largest source of new hires, according to LinkedIn data from intelligence firm Live Data Technologies. Most came from the car maker’s engineering ranks and the pace of hiring Tesla recruits has more than doubled this year, the data shows.

Existing staff at both companies have teamed up on projects in addition to the Roadster. Mr. Musk co-founded xAI in 2023 to compete with A.I. start-ups including OpenAI. Soon after, he announced the company had turned an old factory in Memphis into a giant data center called Colossus to help power the Grok chatbot.

Tesla engineers assisted with the project, which took 122 days. Some staff came from Tesla’s own A.I. data center in Texas, a site that helps power the company’s self-driving software, according to three people familiar with the project. Others came from Dojo, Tesla’s supercomputer project meant to compete directly with Nvidia.

In spring 2025, two engineers from Tesla’s Dojo supercomputer team both worked for both xAI and Tesla, according to internal documents viewed by The New York Times. One of them, Dan Rowland, went on to lead xAI’s data center team before leaving the company in August. Those data centers later accounted for $506 million in Tesla battery purchases.

Earlier this year, Mr. Musk moved an xAI project — to create a digital A.I. agent capable of replacing some white-collar workers — to Tesla’s Autopilot team, three people familiar with the project said. Tesla also hired a handful of xAI engineers to work on the A.I. tool, which was renamed Digital Optimus after the company’s humanoid robot, the people said.

Mr. Musk has said the project is part of Tesla’s $2 billion partnership with xAI, which he recently renamed SpaceXSI.

Mr. Musk has also pushed his companies to use the others’ technology. In July, Mr. Musk sent Tesla employees a companywide email asking them to use Grok as their primary A.I. model, according to a memo viewed by The Times. He told staff that the latest Grok model was lower cost compared with competitors like Anthropic, and asked engineers to directly email him with Grok feedback.

Tesla this year gave staff early access to new versions of the Grok chatbot and coding models for testing. SpaceX’s A.I. unit has been using data from Tesla usage to evaluate its A.I. models and hone them, according to internal communications viewed by The Times.

The companies are only continuing to grow closer. In March, Tesla and SpaceX said they were planning a $16.8 billion joint investment in a chip manufacturing facility in Texas. The project will build the chips that help power SpaceX’s A.I., as well as Tesla’s robotics and autonomous vehicle systems. In the months since, the names of dozens of SpaceX engineers showed up listed in Tesla’s internal organizational charts, according to documents viewed by The Times.

Some engineers at Tesla and SpaceX have considered a merger a foregone conclusion for years. Employees have used an internal chat channel dedicated to discussing Tesla’s stock to hype up a potential deal for months, according to three people familiar with the channel.

Mr. Musk has struck a more cautious tone.

“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” he said last month on a call with investors. “I think that would be overstating it.”

Ryan Mac contributed reporting.
